topics.title: Introduction to Multithreading
topics.description: Learn the basics of Java multithreading, how threads work, how they share memory, and how to avoid common concurrency problems.

sections.title: What is Multithreading?
sections.content:
Multithreading means running multiple threads within the same application. A thread is a small unit of execution that can perform a particular task.

Every Java application starts with a main thread. We can create additional threads when we want different tasks to execute independently.

For example, imagine an application that needs to download a file and process some user input. Instead of making the application wait for the download to finish, these tasks can be handled concurrently using different execution paths.

A simple way to think about it is:

```text
Java Application
       |
       +---- Main Thread
       |
       +---- Worker Thread 1
       |
       +---- Worker Thread 2
       |
       +---- Worker Thread 3
```

Each thread can work on a different task, while all of them belong to the same application.

sections.title: Why Do We Need Multiple Threads?
sections.content:
Without multithreading, an application may need to complete one task before starting another. This can make an application slow or unresponsive, especially when a task spends a lot of time waiting.

For example, suppose an application needs to call an external API. The application might spend several seconds waiting for the API response. During that time, other independent work could potentially continue.

Multithreading is useful for tasks such as:

- Processing multiple web requests
- Reading and writing files
- Calling external APIs
- Processing messages from a queue
- Running background jobs
- Performing calculations
- Handling multiple client connections

The goal is not simply to create as many threads as possible. The goal is to allow independent tasks to make progress efficiently.

sections.title: Thread vs Process
sections.content:
A process is a running instance of an application, while a thread is an execution path inside that process.

For example, when you start a Java application, the operating system creates a process for it. That process can contain multiple threads.

The important difference is memory. Separate processes generally have separate memory spaces, while threads belonging to the same process can share the process's memory.

```text
Process
  |
  +-- Thread 1
  |      Stack
  |
  +-- Thread 2
  |      Stack
  |
  +-- Thread 3
         Stack

Shared by threads:
  Heap
  Objects
  Other process resources
```

Sharing memory makes communication between threads easier, but it also creates problems when multiple threads modify the same data.

sections.title: How Threads Work in Java
Simple Multithreading Example
Concurrency vs Parallelism
sections.content:
Concurrency and parallelism are often used together, but they have different meanings.

Concurrency means multiple tasks can make progress during the same period. The system may switch between tasks while they are running.

Parallelism means multiple tasks are actually executing at the same time, usually on different CPU cores.

For example, imagine two tasks:

```text
Task A: Download file
Task B: Process user request
```

With concurrency, the system can work on Task A, switch to Task B, and then return to Task A when appropriate.

With parallelism on a multi-core CPU, Task A and Task B can actually execute at the same time on different CPU cores.

A useful way to remember the difference is:

```text
Concurrency = dealing with multiple tasks
Parallelism = doing multiple tasks at the same time
```

Multithreading can provide concurrency, and on systems with multiple CPU cores it can also provide parallel execution.

sections.title: Shared Memory and Race Conditions
sections.content:
One of the most important challenges in multithreading is shared data.

Threads in the same process can access objects stored in the heap. If two threads modify the same object at the same time, the result may not be what we expect.

Consider this example:

```java
class Counter {
    int value = 0;

    void increment() {
        value++;
    }
}
```

Suppose two threads call `increment()` on the same Counter object.

It may look like `value++` is one simple operation, but conceptually it involves:

```text
1. Read the current value
2. Add 1
3. Write the new value
```

Imagine the value is 10:

```text
Thread A reads 10
Thread B reads 10
Thread A calculates 11
Thread B calculates 11
Thread A writes 11
Thread B writes 11
```

Two increments happened, but the final value is 11 instead of the expected 12.

This type of problem is called a race condition. The result depends on the timing or ordering of operations performed by multiple threads.

Java provides mechanisms such as `synchronized`, locks, atomic classes, and concurrent collections to safely handle shared data.

sections.title: Thread Safety
sections.content:
Thread safety means that code behaves correctly when multiple threads use it concurrently according to its intended behavior.

One simple way to avoid thread-safety problems is to avoid sharing mutable data whenever possible.

For example, immutable objects are easier to use safely because their state cannot be changed after creation.

Other approaches include:

- Using `synchronized` for critical sections
- Using `AtomicInteger` and other atomic classes
- Using `ReentrantLock` when explicit locking is required
- Using thread-safe collections such as `ConcurrentHashMap`
- Keeping mutable data local to a thread
- Using immutable objects

The important question is not just "How do I create a thread?" but also "What data can this thread access, and can another thread access the same data at the same time?"

sections.title: Does More Threads Mean Better Performance?
sections.content:
No. Creating more threads does not automatically make an application faster.

Every thread requires resources, including memory for its stack. Threads also introduce scheduling and context-switching overhead.

If an application creates too many threads, they may compete for CPU time or wait for the same shared resources. This can actually reduce performance.

The appropriate number of threads depends on the type of workload.

For CPU-bound work, such as heavy calculations, performance is usually related to the number of available CPU cores.

For I/O-bound work, such as database calls, file operations, or network requests, threads may spend significant time waiting. In such cases, having multiple tasks in progress can help the application use its resources more efficiently.

In production Java applications, developers commonly use thread pools and `ExecutorService` instead of creating unlimited threads manually.

topics.title: Creating Threads
topics.description: Learn the different ways to create threads in Java, including extending Thread, implementing Runnable and Callable, and using ExecutorService.

sections.title: Understanding Thread Creation
sections.content:
In Java, a thread represents an independent path of execution. To perform work on a separate thread, we need to define the task and then arrange for that task to be executed by a thread.

Java provides several ways to create and execute threads. The basic approaches are extending the `Thread` class and implementing the `Runnable` interface. For tasks that need to return a result or throw checked exceptions, Java also provides `Callable` and `Future`.

In modern applications, developers usually prefer higher-level APIs such as `ExecutorService` and thread pools instead of creating Thread objects manually for every task.

The important idea is to separate the task from the mechanism used to execute it. `Runnable` and `Callable` describe the work, while an executor can decide which thread should perform that work.

Thread Lifecycle After Creation
sections.content:
After a thread object is created, it does not immediately start executing. The thread needs to be started using `start()`.

A simplified lifecycle looks like this:

```text
NEW
 |
 | start()
 v
RUNNABLE
 |
 | scheduled by JVM/OS
 v
RUNNING
 |
 +---- waiting/blocking ----+
 |                          |
 +--------------------------+
 |
 v
TERMINATED
```

When a Thread object is created, it is initially in the `NEW` state.

After `start()` is called, it moves to a state where it is eligible to run. The JVM and operating system scheduler determine when it gets CPU time.

A thread may temporarily wait because it is sleeping, waiting for another thread, blocked while acquiring a lock, or waiting for another resource.

After the `run()` method finishes, the thread reaches the `TERMINATED` state. A terminated thread cannot be started again.

For example:

```java
Thread thread = new Thread(() -> {
    System.out.println("Running");
});

thread.start();
```

Calling `thread.start()` again after the thread has terminated will result in an `IllegalThreadStateException`.

topics.title: Thread Life Cycle
topics.description: Understand the different states of a Java thread, how a thread moves between states, and how methods such as start(), sleep(), wait(), notify(), and join() affect its lifecycle.

sections.title: What is the Thread Life Cycle?
sections.content:
A thread does not remain in the same state from the moment it is created until it finishes. During its lifetime, a thread moves through different states depending on what it is doing.

For example, a newly created thread has not started yet. After calling `start()`, it becomes eligible to run. It may then run, wait for a lock, sleep for some time, wait for another thread, or eventually finish its work.

Java represents these states using the `Thread.State` enum.

The main thread states are:

```text
NEW
  |
  | start()
  v
RUNNABLE
  |
  +---- running / waiting for CPU
  |
  +---- BLOCKED
  |
  +---- WAITING
  |
  +---- TIMED_WAITING
  |
  v
TERMINATED
```

Understanding these states helps when debugging problems such as a thread that is not running, waiting for a resource, blocked by another thread, or taking too long to complete.

sections.title: NEW State
sections.content:
A thread is in the `NEW` state when a Thread object has been created but `start()` has not been called yet.

For example:

```java
Thread thread = new Thread(() -> {
    System.out.println("Task is running");
});
```

At this point, the Thread object exists, but the thread has not started executing the task.

You can check its state using `getState()`:

```java
System.out.println(thread.getState());
```

The output will be:

```text
NEW
```

Calling `start()` changes the thread from the `NEW` state to `RUNNABLE`.

```java
thread.start();
```

A Thread object in the `NEW` state can be started. However, once a thread has terminated, the same Thread object cannot be started again.

sections.title: RUNNABLE State
sections.content:
After calling `start()`, a thread enters the `RUNNABLE` state.

```java
Thread thread = new Thread(() -> {
    System.out.println("Task is running");
});

thread.start();
```

In Java, `RUNNABLE` represents a thread that is ready to run or is currently running. The Java Thread.State enum does not have a separate `RUNNING` state.

The operating system scheduler decides when the thread gets CPU time. Therefore, calling `start()` does not mean that the thread immediately executes.

For example:

```text
Thread A -> RUNNABLE
Thread B -> RUNNABLE
Thread C -> RUNNABLE

        |
        v
   CPU Scheduler
        |
        v
   CPU executes one or more threads
```

A thread may remain in the `RUNNABLE` state while waiting for CPU time. After getting CPU time, it executes its task.

This is an important interview point: Java's `RUNNABLE` state covers both a thread that is ready to run and one that is actually running.

sections.title: BLOCKED State
sections.content:
A thread enters the `BLOCKED` state when it is waiting to acquire a monitor lock so that it can enter a synchronized block or method.

Consider this example:

```java
class SharedResource {
    synchronized void process() {
        System.out.println("Processing...");
    }
}
```

Suppose Thread A enters the synchronized method and holds the object's monitor lock. If Thread B tries to enter the same synchronized method while Thread A still holds the lock, Thread B cannot enter the method immediately.

Thread B becomes `BLOCKED` while waiting for the monitor lock.

```text
Thread A
   |
   v
Acquires lock
   |
   v
Running inside synchronized method

Thread B
   |
   v
Tries to acquire same lock
   |
   v
BLOCKED
   |
   | Thread A releases lock
   v
RUNNABLE
```

`BLOCKED` specifically relates to waiting for a monitor lock. It should not be confused with `WAITING` or `TIMED_WAITING`.

sections.title: WAITING State
TIMED_WAITING State
TERMINATED State
Complete Thread Life Cycle
Important Thread Methods
sections.content:
Several Java methods are commonly associated with thread lifecycle management.

`start()` starts a new thread and causes its `run()` method to execute on that thread.

`run()` contains the task logic. Calling it directly is just a normal method call and does not start a new thread.

`sleep()` pauses the current thread for a specified period and puts it into `TIMED_WAITING`. It does not release locks that the thread already holds.

`join()` allows one thread to wait for another thread to finish. Without a timeout, the waiting thread can enter `WAITING`; with a timeout, it can enter `TIMED_WAITING`.

`wait()` causes the current thread to wait for another thread to signal it. It must be called while the thread owns the relevant object's monitor, normally inside a synchronized block or method.

`notify()` wakes one thread waiting on the same object's monitor, while `notifyAll()` wakes all threads waiting on that monitor. Waking does not mean the thread immediately runs; it still needs to reacquire the monitor before continuing.

`interrupt()` requests that a thread stop what it is waiting or doing, depending on the operation and how the task handles interruption. It does not forcibly kill the thread.

topics.title: Thread Priorities
topics.description: Learn how Java thread priorities work, how priority values affect thread scheduling, and why thread priority should not be used to guarantee execution order.

sections.title: What are Thread Priorities?
Priority Values in Java
sections.content:
Java supports ten priority levels, from 1 to 10.

```text
Priority 1  -> MIN_PRIORITY
Priority 2
Priority 3
Priority 4
Priority 5  -> NORM_PRIORITY
Priority 6
Priority 7
Priority 8
Priority 9
Priority 10 -> MAX_PRIORITY
```

The commonly used constants are:

```java
Thread.MIN_PRIORITY
Thread.NORM_PRIORITY
Thread.MAX_PRIORITY
```

Their values are:

```java
System.out.println(Thread.MIN_PRIORITY);   // 1
System.out.println(Thread.NORM_PRIORITY);  // 5
System.out.println(Thread.MAX_PRIORITY);   // 10
```

Most application threads normally use the default priority of 5. You can assign another value when there is a specific reason to provide a different scheduling hint.

The valid priority range is 1 through 10. Attempting to set a value outside this range results in an `IllegalArgumentException`.

sections.title: Setting Thread Priority
Simple Thread Priority Example
Does Higher Priority Mean First Execution?
Thread Priority and Scheduling
sections.content:
Thread scheduling determines which runnable thread gets CPU time. Java exposes thread priority, but the actual scheduling behavior can depend on the underlying operating system and JVM implementation.

On some systems, priority may influence scheduling more noticeably than on others. The JVM does not provide a portable guarantee that a higher-priority Java thread will always receive CPU time before a lower-priority thread.

For example, suppose three threads are ready to execute:

```text
Thread A -> Priority 3
Thread B -> Priority 5
Thread C -> Priority 9
```

It is tempting to assume that Thread C will always execute first, followed by B and then A. That assumption is unsafe.

Other factors can influence scheduling, including CPU availability, operating system scheduling policies, blocking, waiting, I/O operations, and system load.

Therefore, thread priority should generally be treated as an optional tuning mechanism rather than a fundamental part of application correctness.

sections.title: Priority Inheritance
Priority and Starvation
sections.content:
Starvation occurs when a thread is repeatedly unable to get the resources or CPU time it needs to make reasonable progress.

In scheduling scenarios, giving some threads consistently higher priority can contribute to situations where lower-priority work receives less opportunity to execute. The exact behavior depends on the operating system and JVM, so priority should not be treated as a guaranteed starvation mechanism.

For example, imagine a system with a high-priority task that continuously consumes CPU resources while a lower-priority task is also ready to run. Depending on the scheduler, the lower-priority task may receive less CPU time.

This is one reason why thread priority should be used carefully. If tasks have important correctness or fairness requirements, use explicit concurrency mechanisms and appropriate executor configuration rather than relying only on thread priorities.

topics.shortDescription: Understand Java thread priorities, priority values, priority inheritance, scheduling behavior, and why priority should not be used for synchronization.

topics.title: Thread Synchronization
topics.description: Learn how thread synchronization prevents multiple threads from incorrectly modifying shared data at the same time and how Java provides synchronized methods, synchronized blocks, locks, and other mechanisms for safe concurrent access.

sections.title: What is Thread Synchronization?
sections.content:
Thread synchronization is a mechanism used to control how multiple threads access shared data or resources.

When multiple threads work with the same object or variable, they may try to read or modify that data at the same time. If the operations are not coordinated properly, the final result can be incorrect or unpredictable.

For example, suppose two threads are updating the same bank account balance:

```text
Initial balance = ₹1000

Thread A -> withdraw ₹100
Thread B -> withdraw ₹200
```

Both threads may read the balance before either thread updates it. If the operations are not properly coordinated, one update can overwrite another update.

Synchronization helps ensure that only the appropriate thread can execute a critical section at a particular time.

A simple way to think about synchronization is:

```text
Without synchronization:

Thread A -----> Shared Data <----- Thread B
                    |
              Both access it
              at the same time

With synchronization:

Thread A -----> [ LOCK ] -----> Shared Data
Thread B -------- waits ---------|
                                  |
                           A releases lock
                                  |
Thread B -----> [ LOCK ] -----> Shared Data
```

The goal is not necessarily to prevent all threads from running simultaneously. The goal is to protect operations that must be coordinated when accessing shared state.

sections.title: Why Do We Need Synchronization?
sections.content:
Synchronization is needed when multiple threads access shared mutable data and at least one of them can modify that data.

Consider a simple counter:

```java
class Counter {
    int count = 0;

    void increment() {
        count++;
    }
}
```

Now suppose two threads call `increment()` many times.

It may seem that if each thread increments the counter 1000 times, the final result should always be 2000. However, that result is not guaranteed because `count++` involves multiple steps.

Conceptually:

```text
1. Read count
2. Add 1
3. Write count
```

A possible execution is:

```text
Thread A reads count = 10
Thread B reads count = 10
Thread A calculates 11
Thread B calculates 11
Thread A writes 11
Thread B writes 11
```

Two increments were attempted, but the final value is 11 instead of 12.

This is called a race condition.

Synchronization can ensure that the increment operation is performed by one thread at a time when that is the required design.

sections.title: Critical Section
Synchronized Method
Synchronized Block
Instance Lock vs Static Lock
sections.content:
Synchronization behaves differently for instance methods and static methods.

A synchronized instance method locks the monitor associated with the particular object.

```java
public synchronized void process() {
    // instance lock
}
```

If two threads call this method on the same object, they cannot execute the synchronized method simultaneously.

However, they can execute it at the same time if they are using different objects:

```java
Service service1 = new Service();
Service service2 = new Service();
```

A synchronized static method locks the monitor associated with the Class object.

```java
public static synchronized void process() {
    // class-level lock
}
```

Therefore, a synchronized static method uses a class-level monitor rather than an individual object monitor.

A useful way to remember this is:

```text
synchronized instance method
        -> lock on this object

synchronized static method
        -> lock on the Class object
```

Understanding which object is being locked is important when diagnosing synchronization problems.

sections.title: How synchronized Works
sections.content:
The `synchronized` keyword is based on Java's monitor mechanism.

When a thread enters a synchronized method or block, it must acquire the associated monitor. If another thread already owns that monitor, the second thread cannot enter the protected section and may enter the `BLOCKED` state while waiting for the monitor.

A simplified sequence looks like this:

```text
Thread A
   |
   v
Acquire monitor
   |
   v
Execute synchronized code
   |
   v
Release monitor

Thread B
   |
   v
Try to acquire monitor
   |
   v
Wait if monitor is unavailable
   |
   v
Acquire monitor
   |
   v
Execute synchronized code
```

When the synchronized block or method finishes normally, the monitor is released. If the protected code exits because of an exception, the monitor is also released as the synchronized construct is exited.

Synchronization also provides memory-visibility guarantees. Changes made by one thread before releasing a monitor can become visible to another thread after it successfully acquires the same monitor.

sections.title: Synchronization and Memory Visibility
Synchronization Example
Synchronization vs Atomic Operations
Synchronization vs volatile
sections.content:
The `volatile` keyword and synchronization solve different problems.

`volatile` provides visibility guarantees for a variable between threads, but it does not make compound operations automatically atomic.

For example:

```java
private volatile int count;
```

This does not make the following operation thread-safe:

```java
count++;
```

The increment still involves reading the value, adding one, and writing the result.

Synchronization, on the other hand, can provide both mutual exclusion and memory-visibility guarantees.

A simple comparison is:

```text
volatile
  -> visibility
  -> does not make count++ atomic

synchronized
  -> mutual exclusion
  -> visibility guarantees
  -> protects a critical section
```

Choosing between these mechanisms depends on the exact concurrency requirement.

sections.title: Common Synchronization Problems
sections.content:
Synchronization solves some concurrency problems, but incorrect synchronization can introduce new problems.

One common problem is excessive locking. If too much code is synchronized, threads may spend significant time waiting for locks, reducing concurrency and performance.

Another problem is deadlock. A deadlock can occur when two or more threads wait for locks held by each other.

For example:

```text
Thread A holds Lock 1
Thread A waits for Lock 2

Thread B holds Lock 2
Thread B waits for Lock 1

        |
        v
     DEADLOCK
```

Another problem is lock contention. When many threads frequently compete for the same lock, they may spend more time waiting than performing useful work.

There can also be problems when different parts of an application use different locks for the same shared data. Synchronization only helps when threads follow a consistent locking strategy.

Good synchronization design therefore requires identifying the shared state, selecting an appropriate lock or concurrency mechanism, and keeping the protected region as small and clear as practical.

modules.title: Unit II: Collection Framework
modules.description: Use Java collections to store, search, traverse, sort, and manage groups of objects.

topics.title: Collection Framework
topics.description: Learn the Java Collection Framework, its core interfaces and implementations, and how to choose the right collection for different programming requirements.

sections.title: What is the Collection Framework?
sections.content:
The Java Collection Framework is a set of interfaces, classes, and utility methods that make it easier to store, retrieve, and manipulate groups of objects.

Instead of creating your own data structures for every application, Java provides ready-to-use collections such as `ArrayList`, `LinkedList`, `HashSet`, `TreeSet`, `HashMap`, and `TreeMap`.

For example, suppose an application needs to store the names of several employees. Instead of creating separate variables:

```java
String employee1 = "Rahul";
String employee2 = "Priya";
String employee3 = "Amit";
```

we can use a collection:

```java
List<String> employees = new ArrayList<>();

employees.add("Rahul");
employees.add("Priya");
employees.add("Amit");
```

The Collection Framework provides common operations such as adding elements, removing elements, searching, sorting, and iterating over data.

A simple mental model is:

```text
Java Collection Framework
          |
    +-----+------+
    |            |
 Collection     Map
    |            |
 List Set     HashMap
 Queue         TreeMap
              LinkedHashMap
```

One important point is that `Map` is part of the Java Collection Framework, but it does not extend the `Collection` interface.

sections.title: Why Do We Need Collections?
Collection Framework Hierarchy
sections.content:
The main interfaces in the Collection Framework are `List`, `Set`, and `Queue`. The `Map` interface represents key-value mappings and is separate from the `Collection` interface.

A simplified hierarchy looks like this:

```text
                    Iterable
                       |
                   Collection
                       |
          +------------+------------+
          |            |            |
         List          Set         Queue
          |             |            |
     ArrayList       HashSet     PriorityQueue
     LinkedList      LinkedHashSet
     Vector          TreeSet
                    
                    Map
                     |
          +----------+----------+
          |          |          |
       HashMap   LinkedHashMap TreeMap
```

The hierarchy helps you understand what behavior a collection provides.

`List` is generally used when order and positional access matter.

`Set` is used when duplicate elements should not be allowed.

`Queue` is used when elements need to be processed according to a particular ordering or queueing policy.

`Map` is used when data needs to be stored as key-value pairs.

sections.title: List Interface
ArrayList
LinkedList
Set Interface
sections.content:
The `Set` interface represents a collection that does not allow duplicate elements according to the set's equality rules.

For example:

```java
Set<String> names = new HashSet<>();

names.add("Amit");
names.add("Priya");
names.add("Amit");

System.out.println(names);
```

The second `Amit` is not added because the set does not allow duplicates.

Common Set implementations include:

- `HashSet`
- `LinkedHashSet`
- `TreeSet`

These implementations have different ordering behavior.

`HashSet` does not guarantee iteration order.

`LinkedHashSet` maintains insertion order during iteration.

`TreeSet` maintains elements according to their sorted ordering.

Choose a Set when uniqueness is the primary requirement rather than positional access.

sections.title: HashSet
sections.content:
`HashSet` is a commonly used Set implementation that uses hashing internally.

```java
Set<Integer> numbers = new HashSet<>();

numbers.add(10);
numbers.add(20);
numbers.add(10);

System.out.println(numbers);
```

Only one `10` is stored.

HashSet generally provides expected O(1) time for basic operations such as `add()`, `remove()`, and `contains()`, assuming a good distribution of hash codes and a properly functioning hash table.

HashSet does not guarantee iteration order.

When objects are stored in a HashSet, their `equals()` and `hashCode()` implementations are important because hashing and equality are used to determine whether elements should be considered duplicates.

A fundamental rule is:

```text
If two objects are equal according to equals(),
they must return the same hashCode().
```

Breaking this contract can lead to unexpected collection behavior.

sections.title: LinkedHashSet and TreeSet
Queue and Deque
Map Interface
sections.content:
A `Map` stores data as key-value pairs. Unlike List and Set, Map does not extend the `Collection` interface.

For example:

```java
Map<Integer, String> employees = new HashMap<>();

employees.put(101, "Amit");
employees.put(102, "Priya");

System.out.println(employees.get(101));
```

Output:

```text
Amit
```

Here, `101` is the key and `Amit` is the corresponding value.

Keys are unique within a Map. If you insert another value using an existing key, the previous value is replaced.

```java
employees.put(101, "Rahul");
```

Now key 101 maps to Rahul.

Common Map implementations include:

- `HashMap`
- `LinkedHashMap`
- `TreeMap`
- `ConcurrentHashMap`

Maps are useful when data needs to be looked up using a unique key, such as finding a user by ID or a product by product code.

sections.title: HashMap
sections.content:
`HashMap` is one of the most commonly used Map implementations in Java. It stores key-value pairs using hashing.

```java
Map<String, Integer> scores = new HashMap<>();

scores.put("Amit", 90);
scores.put("Priya", 95);
scores.put("Rahul", 85);

System.out.println(scores.get("Priya"));
```

The result is:

```text
95
```

HashMap provides expected O(1) time for basic `put()` and `get()` operations under typical conditions.

HashMap allows one null key and multiple null values. It does not guarantee iteration order.

HashMap uses the key's `hashCode()` to determine where an entry should be stored and uses `equals()` to distinguish keys that have the same hash bucket.

Therefore, custom objects used as keys should correctly implement both `equals()` and `hashCode()`.

A HashMap is a good choice when you primarily need fast key-based lookup and do not require sorted or insertion order.

sections.title: LinkedHashMap and TreeMap
Iterator and Enhanced for Loop
Sorting Collections
Collections and Generics
sections.content:
Java collections work closely with generics. Generics allow you to specify the type of elements that a collection can contain.

Without generics:

```java
List names = new ArrayList();
names.add("Amit");
names.add(100);
```

This allows different types and can result in runtime type problems.

With generics:

```java
List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();
names.add("Amit");
names.add("Priya");
```

Now the compiler prevents values of incompatible types from being added.

```java
names.add(100); // Compilation error
```

Generics provide compile-time type safety and reduce the need for explicit casting when retrieving elements.

For example:

```java
String name = names.get(0);
```

The compiler already knows that the list contains String objects.

sections.title: Choosing the Right Collection
sections.content:
Choosing a collection depends on what your application needs.

If you need an ordered list with fast index-based access, `ArrayList` is usually a good starting point.

If you need unique elements and do not care about iteration order, `HashSet` is commonly used.

If you need unique elements while preserving insertion order, use `LinkedHashSet`.

If you need unique elements in sorted order, use `TreeSet`.

If you need key-value lookup with no ordering requirement, `HashMap` is a common choice.

If you need predictable insertion-order iteration for a map, use `LinkedHashMap`.

If you need keys in sorted order, use `TreeMap`.

If you need queue or stack-like operations, `ArrayDeque` is often a good choice.

A simple decision guide is:

```text
Need duplicates?
   |
   +-- Yes -> List
   |           |
   |           +-- Fast index access -> ArrayList
   |
   +-- No -> Set
               |
               +-- No ordering -> HashSet
               +-- Insertion order -> LinkedHashSet
               +-- Sorted order -> TreeSet

Need key-value pairs?
   |
   +-- No ordering -> HashMap
   +-- Insertion order -> LinkedHashMap
   +-- Sorted keys -> TreeMap
```

The best collection is determined by the operations your application performs most frequently, not simply by memorizing one implementation as universally fastest.

sections.title: Thread-Safe Collections
sections.content:
Most commonly used collections such as `ArrayList`, `HashMap`, and `HashSet` are not designed for unsynchronized concurrent modification by multiple threads.

When multiple threads need to access shared collections concurrently, Java provides several options.

For example, `ConcurrentHashMap` is designed for concurrent access:

```java
Map<String, Integer> map = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

map.put("A", 100);
map.put("B", 200);
```

Other options include concurrent queues such as `ConcurrentLinkedQueue` and copy-on-write collections such as `CopyOnWriteArrayList` for workloads where reads are frequent and modifications are relatively infrequent.

Java also provides wrappers such as:

```java
List<String> list = Collections.synchronizedList(new ArrayList<>());
```

However, synchronization requirements still need to be considered when performing multiple operations as one logical action.

The key point is that choosing a collection for concurrent access depends on the access pattern, not simply on whether the collection has a synchronized wrapper.

topics.shortDescription: Understand Java Collection Framework interfaces and implementations such as List, Set, Queue, HashMap, ArrayList, HashSet, and TreeMap, and learn when to use each one.

topics.title: Collection Interface
topics.description: Learn the Collection interface in Java, its hierarchy, core methods, implementations, and how it is used to work with groups of objects.

sections.title: What Is the Collection Interface?
Collection Interface Hierarchy
sections.content:
The Collection interface is the parent interface for several important collection types in Java.

The simplified hierarchy looks like this:

```text
                    Iterable
                       |
                  Collection
                 /    |      \
                /     |       \
             List     Set     Queue
              |        |        |
        ArrayList   HashSet   PriorityQueue
        LinkedList  TreeSet   Deque
        Vector      LinkedHashSet
```

The major interfaces are:

- List: Allows duplicate elements and generally maintains insertion order.
- Set: Does not allow duplicate elements.
- Queue: Designed for processing elements, often in a particular order.
- Deque: Supports insertion and removal from both ends.

Some common implementations are:

```text
List
 ├── ArrayList
 ├── LinkedList
 └── Vector

Set
 ├── HashSet
 ├── LinkedHashSet
 └── TreeSet

Queue
 ├── PriorityQueue
 └── LinkedList

Deque
 ├── ArrayDeque
 └── LinkedList
```

Map such as HashMap and TreeMap is part of the Collections Framework, but Map does not extend Collection. This is a common interview question.

```text
Collection
   ├── List
   ├── Set
   └── Queue

Map    <-- separate hierarchy
```

sections.title: Why Use the Collection Interface?
Important Methods of Collection
Adding and Removing Elements
Traversing a Collection
Collection and Generics
Collection vs Collections
sections.content:
Collection and Collections are different things, even though their names look very similar.

### Collection
Collection is an interface.

```java
Collection<String> names = new ArrayList<>();
```

It defines common operations for groups of objects.

### Collections
Collections is a utility class in java.util that provides static helper methods for working with collections.

```java
Collections.sort(names);
Collections.reverse(names);
```

A simple comparison is:

```text
Collection
    -> Interface
    -> Represents a group of objects

Collections
    -> Utility class
    -> Provides helper methods
```

For example:

```java
List<Integer> numbers = new ArrayList<>();
numbers.add(30);
numbers.add(10);
numbers.add(20);

Collections.sort(numbers);

System.out.println(numbers);
```

This distinction is frequently asked in Java interviews.

sections.title: Collection vs Map
sections.content:
A common interview question is whether Map is a Collection.

The answer is no. Map does not extend the Collection interface.

Collection represents a group of individual elements:

```text
Collection
   -> Element
   -> Element
   -> Element
```

Map represents key-value associations:

```text
Map
   -> Key -> Value
   -> Key -> Value
   -> Key -> Value
```

For example:

```java
Collection<String> names = new ArrayList<>();
names.add("Amit");
names.add("Neha");
```

With Map:

```java
Map<Integer, String> employees = new HashMap<>();
employees.put(101, "Amit");
employees.put(102, "Neha");
```

Map has its own operations such as put(), get(), containsKey(), and containsValue().

Although Map is not a Collection, the Collections Framework includes both Collection-based interfaces and Map-based interfaces.

sections.title: Null Elements and Collection Implementations
Collection and Streams
sections.content:
Collections and the Stream API are often used together in modern Java applications.

A Collection stores elements, while a Stream provides a way to process those elements.

For example:

```java
List<Integer> numbers = Arrays.asList(10, 20, 30, 40, 50);

List<Integer> result = numbers.stream()
        .filter(n -> n > 20)
        .toList();

System.out.println(result);
```

The collection contains the data. The stream describes the processing operation.

A useful mental model is:

```text
Collection
    |
    | stream()
    v
Stream
    |
    +--> filter()
    +--> map()
    +--> sorted()
    +--> collect()/toList()
```

Streams do not replace collections. They are commonly used to process data that is stored in collections.

This distinction becomes important when discussing Java 8+ interview questions.

topics.shortDescription: Understand Java's Collection interface, its hierarchy, common methods, implementations, and practical usage.

topics.title: ArrayList
topics.description: Learn how Java ArrayList works, including its internal structure, resizing, common operations, performance, iteration, and practical use cases.

sections.title: What Is ArrayList?
ArrayList Hierarchy
sections.content:
ArrayList implements the List interface and ultimately belongs to the Collection hierarchy.

A simplified hierarchy is:

```text
Iterable
   |
Collection
   |
List
   |
ArrayList
```

ArrayList also implements the RandomAccess interface, which indicates that indexed access can be performed efficiently.

A simplified class relationship is:

```text
AbstractCollection
        |
   AbstractList
        |
    ArrayList
```

ArrayList implements several interfaces, including:

- List
- RandomAccess
- Cloneable
- Serializable

In normal application code, it is common to declare the variable using the List interface:

```java
List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();
```

instead of:

```java
ArrayList<String> names = new ArrayList<>();
```

Using the interface makes the code less dependent on a particular implementation when the ArrayList-specific API is not required.

sections.title: How ArrayList Stores Elements Internally
sections.content:
ArrayList is backed by an internal array. You can think of it conceptually as:

```text
ArrayList
   |
   v
Internal array
+-----+-----+-----+-----+-----+
| 10  | 20  | 30  | 40  | ... |
+-----+-----+-----+-----+-----+
   0     1     2     3
```

When you call add(), ArrayList places the element into the next available position.

```java
List<Integer> numbers = new ArrayList<>();

numbers.add(10);
numbers.add(20);
numbers.add(30);
```

Conceptually:

```text
Index:    0     1     2
Value:   10    20    30
```

When you call get(1), ArrayList can directly access the element at index 1.

```java
System.out.println(numbers.get(1));
```

Output:

```text
20
```

This direct indexed access is one of the main reasons ArrayList is efficient for read-heavy use cases.

The actual internal implementation details can vary between Java releases, so interview answers should focus on the important concept: ArrayList uses a dynamically resized array as its backing storage.

sections.title: Size vs Capacity
sections.content:
One important ArrayList concept is the difference between size and capacity.

Size means the number of elements currently stored in the list.

Capacity means how many elements the current internal array can hold before it needs to be resized.

For example:

```java
ArrayList<String> names = new ArrayList<>();

names.add("Amit");
names.add("Neha");
```

The size is 2. The internal capacity may be larger than 2.

Conceptually:

```text
Size = 2

Capacity = more than 2

+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
| Amit  | Neha  | empty | empty | empty |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
```

The public size() method tells you the number of stored elements:

```java
System.out.println(names.size());
```

Capacity is an implementation detail and is not directly returned by the List interface.

If you know that a large number of elements will be added, you can provide an initial capacity when constructing an ArrayList:

```java
ArrayList<String> names = new ArrayList<>(1000);
```

This can reduce the number of internal array resizing operations when many elements are added.

sections.title: How ArrayList Grows
sections.content:
An ArrayList cannot keep adding elements after its internal array becomes full. When more space is required, it creates a larger array and copies the existing elements into it.

Conceptually:

```text
Before resizing:

[10][20][30][40]
             Full

        |
        | Create larger array
        v

After resizing:

[10][20][30][40][ ][ ][ ]
```

The exact growth policy is an implementation detail and should not be treated as a universal fixed number across all Java versions.

The important idea is that adding an element can occasionally require an expensive resize and copy operation. However, because resizing does not happen for every insertion, append operations have amortized constant-time behavior.

For example:

```java
List<Integer> numbers = new ArrayList<>();

for (int i = 0; i < 100000; i++) {
    numbers.add(i);
}
```

ArrayList handles the growth automatically.

If the approximate number of elements is known in advance, specifying an initial capacity can help avoid unnecessary resizing:

```java
ArrayList<Integer> numbers = new ArrayList<>(100000);
```

sections.title: Adding Elements to ArrayList
sections.content:
ArrayList provides several ways to add elements.

### add(element)

Adds an element at the end of the list.

```java
List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();

names.add("Amit");
names.add("Neha");
names.add("Raj");
```

The result is:

```text
[Amit, Neha, Raj]
```

### add(index, element)

Adds an element at a particular index.

```java
names.add(1, "Priya");
```

Now the list becomes:

```text
[Amit, Priya, Neha, Raj]
```

When an element is inserted in the middle, elements after that position must be shifted to make room.

For example:

```text
Before:
[A][B][C][D]

Insert X at index 1:

[A][X][B][C][D]
```

This shifting is why inserting into the middle of an ArrayList is generally slower than appending at the end.

### addAll()

You can add all elements from another collection:

```java
List<String> additionalNames = List.of("Karan", "Ravi");
names.addAll(additionalNames);
```

This is useful when combining multiple collections.

sections.title: Accessing and Updating Elements
sections.content:
ArrayList provides index-based access through get() and set().

### get()

Use get(index) to retrieve an element:

```java
List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();
names.add("Amit");
names.add("Neha");
names.add("Raj");

String name = names.get(1);
System.out.println(name);
```

Output:

```text
Neha
```

ArrayList provides efficient indexed access because it uses an array internally.

### set()

Use set(index, element) to replace an existing element:

```java
names.set(1, "Priya");
```

The list becomes:

```text
[Amit, Priya, Raj]
```

Unlike add(index, element), set() does not insert a new element. It replaces the existing element at that index.

This distinction is frequently tested in interviews:

```text
add(index, value)
    -> inserts a new element
    -> list size increases

set(index, value)
    -> replaces existing element
    -> list size does not change
```

sections.title: Removing Elements
Searching in ArrayList
ArrayList and Null Values
ArrayList and Iteration
Time Complexity of ArrayList
sections.content:
Understanding ArrayList performance is important for interviews.

Typical complexity is:

```text
Operation                  Typical Complexity
------------------------------------------------
get(index)                 O(1)
set(index, value)          O(1)
add(value) at end          O(1) amortized
add(index, value)          O(n)
remove(index)              O(n)
remove(object)             O(n)
contains(object)           O(n)
indexOf(object)            O(n)
```

Why is get() O(1)?

Because ArrayList uses an array, it can calculate the memory position of an indexed element directly.

Why is insertion in the middle O(n)?

Elements after the insertion point have to be shifted.

```text
Before:
[A][B][C][D][E]

Insert X at index 2:

[A][B][X][C][D][E]
          <- elements shifted
```

Why is remove(index) O(n)?

After an element is removed, elements after it generally need to be shifted toward the beginning of the array.

The append operation is usually described as O(1) amortized because occasional resizing can take O(n), but those expensive resize operations are spread across many additions.

sections.title: ArrayList vs LinkedList
sections.content:
ArrayList and LinkedList both implement List, but they use different internal data structures and therefore have different performance characteristics.

```text
ArrayList
   -> Dynamic array
   -> Fast indexed access
   -> Insertion/removal in middle may require shifting

LinkedList
   -> Linked nodes
   -> Indexed access requires traversal
   -> Insertion/removal can be efficient when the relevant node position is already known
```

Example:

```java
List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();
```

is generally a good choice when you frequently access elements by index.

For example:

```java
String name = names.get(500);
```

ArrayList is designed for efficient indexed access.

However, choosing LinkedList simply because you heard that insertion is O(1) can be misleading. Finding the position in a LinkedList can itself require traversal. In many real applications, ArrayList is the natural default for List unless the application's access pattern gives a clear reason to choose another implementation.

Interviewers often expect you to explain the workload rather than simply saying one collection is always better.

sections.title: ArrayList vs Array
sections.content:
A Java array and ArrayList both store multiple values, but they are designed for different situations.

### Array

```java
String[] names = new String[3];
```

The size is fixed when the array is created.

### ArrayList

```java
List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();
```

The list can grow and shrink dynamically.

Important differences:

```text
Array
- Fixed size
- Can store primitives directly
- Simple and lightweight
- Uses [] syntax for indexed access

ArrayList
- Dynamic size
- Stores objects, using wrapper types for primitives
- Provides collection methods such as add(), remove(), contains()
- Integrates with the Collections Framework
```

For example, an ArrayList of integers uses Integer objects:

```java
List<Integer> numbers = new ArrayList<>();
numbers.add(10);
```

Java handles the conversion between int and Integer through autoboxing in this situation.

Use an array when a fixed-size structure is appropriate or when an API specifically requires an array. Use ArrayList when you need a dynamic list with the standard List operations.

sections.title: Is ArrayList Thread-Safe?
Fail-Fast Iterators and ConcurrentModificationException
Useful ArrayList Methods
sections.content:
Some ArrayList/List methods are used frequently in real projects and interviews.

```java
List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();

names.add("Amit");
names.add("Neha");
names.add("Raj");
```

Common operations include:

```java
names.size();                 // Number of elements
names.isEmpty();              // Whether list is empty
names.get(0);                 // Element at index 0
names.set(0, "Ravi");         // Replace element
names.add("Karan");           // Add at end
names.add(1, "Priya");        // Insert at index
names.remove(0);              // Remove by index
names.remove("Raj");         // Remove by object
names.contains("Neha");       // Search
names.indexOf("Neha");        // First matching index
names.clear();                // Remove everything
```

ArrayList also supports methods inherited through List and Collection, so learning the List and Collection contracts is important when working with ArrayList.

sections.title: When Should You Use ArrayList?
sections.content:
ArrayList is a good fit when your application needs a dynamic list and frequently reads elements by index.

Typical examples include:

- Storing search results returned from a service.
- Keeping a list of users or products.
- Holding database query results.
- Maintaining an ordered collection of objects.
- Processing a sequence of items using the Stream API.
- Building a temporary list while processing data.

For example:

```java
List<String> products = new ArrayList<>();

products.add("Laptop");
products.add("Phone");
products.add("Monitor");

for (String product : products) {
    System.out.println(product);
}
```

ArrayList is particularly convenient when:

```text
Frequent indexed reads       -> Good fit
Duplicates allowed            -> Good fit
Insertion order matters       -> Good fit
Mostly append at the end      -> Good fit
Frequent middle insert/remove -> Consider alternatives
Need unique elements          -> Consider Set
Need key-value lookup         -> Consider Map
```

The correct collection should always be selected according to the application's actual access and modification patterns.

topics.shortDescription: Understand ArrayList, its dynamic-array implementation, common operations, performance characteristics, and practical use cases.

topics.title: Vector
topics.description: Learn how Java Vector works, including its dynamic array structure, synchronization, capacity management, performance, common methods, and differences from ArrayList.

sections.title: What Is Vector?
sections.content:
Vector is a legacy collection class in Java that implements the List interface. Like ArrayList, it stores elements in a dynamically growing array.

Vector belongs to the java.util package:

```java
import java.util.Vector;
```

A simple example is:

```java
Vector<String> names = new Vector<>();

names.add("Amit");
names.add("Neha");
names.add("Rahul");

System.out.println(names);
```

Output:

```text
[Amit, Neha, Rahul]
```

Vector maintains insertion order, allows duplicate elements, and allows null values.

The most important difference from ArrayList is that Vector's legacy element-access and modification methods are synchronized. This gives it thread-safety for individual method calls, but it also introduces synchronization overhead.

Vector was introduced in early versions of Java, before the modern Collections Framework. It was later retrofitted to implement the List interface.

In new code, ArrayList is generally preferred when synchronization is not required. If concurrent access is required, modern concurrent collection classes may be a better fit depending on the use case.

sections.title: Vector Hierarchy
sections.content:
Vector is part of the List hierarchy.

A simplified hierarchy is:

```text
Iterable
   |
Collection
   |
List
   |
Vector
```

Vector also extends AbstractList and implements several interfaces, including List, RandomAccess, Cloneable, and Serializable.

Conceptually:

```text
AbstractCollection
        |
   AbstractList
        |
      Vector
```

Because Vector implements List, it provides common List operations such as add(), get(), set(), remove(), contains(), and size().

Example:

```java
List<String> names = new Vector<>();
```

This is valid because Vector is a List implementation.

Using the List interface as the reference type allows code to work with different List implementations when only List behavior is required.

sections.title: How Vector Stores Elements
sections.content:
Vector uses an internal array to store its elements. The array can grow when the current capacity is not enough.

Conceptually:

```text
Vector
   |
   v
Internal array
+-----+-----+-----+-----+-----+
| 10  | 20  | 30  | 40  | ... |
+-----+-----+-----+-----+-----+
   0     1     2     3
```

When you add an element:

```java
Vector<Integer> numbers = new Vector<>();

numbers.add(10);
numbers.add(20);
numbers.add(30);
```

The values are stored in index order:

```text
Index:    0     1     2
Value:   10    20    30
```

Because Vector is array-backed, accessing an element by index is typically O(1):

```java
System.out.println(numbers.get(1));
```

Output:

```text
20
```

When more elements need to be stored than the current internal array can hold, Vector increases its capacity and moves the existing elements into the new storage.

sections.title: Vector Size and Capacity
sections.content:
Vector has two related but different concepts: size and capacity.

Size is the number of elements currently stored in the Vector.

Capacity is the amount of storage available before Vector needs to grow its internal array.

Example:

```java
Vector<String> names = new Vector<>(10);

names.add("Amit");
names.add("Neha");

System.out.println(names.size());
System.out.println(names.capacity());
```

The size is 2, while the initial capacity is 10.

Conceptually:

```text
Size = 2
Capacity = 10

[Amit][Neha][ ][ ][ ][ ][ ][ ][ ][ ]
```

Vector provides the capacity() method, unlike the List interface.

You can also inspect the current capacity:

```java
int capacity = names.capacity();
```

If more elements are added than the current capacity can hold, Vector grows automatically.

sections.title: How Vector Grows
sections.content:
Vector can automatically increase its capacity when its internal array becomes full.

Unlike ArrayList, Vector exposes an explicit capacityIncrement setting that can influence how the capacity grows.

For example:

```java
Vector<Integer> numbers = new Vector<>(3, 2);
```

Here:

```text
Initial capacity      = 3
Capacity increment    = 2
```

Conceptually, when the Vector becomes full, its capacity can grow from 3 to 5, then from 5 to 7, and so on.

You can also create a Vector without specifying a capacity increment:

```java
Vector<Integer> numbers = new Vector<>();
```

In that case, Vector uses its default growth policy.

The exact implementation behavior should not be relied upon as an application-level contract. The important interview distinction is that Vector supports a configurable capacity increment, whereas ArrayList has its own implementation-defined growth strategy.

You can explicitly increase capacity using:

```java
numbers.ensureCapacity(100);
```

This can be useful when you know that a large number of elements will be added.

sections.title: Adding Elements to Vector
sections.content:
Vector supports the normal List methods for adding elements.

### add()

Adds an element at the end:

```java
Vector<String> names = new Vector<>();

names.add("Amit");
names.add("Neha");
```

### add(index, element)

Inserts an element at a specific position:

```java
names.add(1, "Priya");
```

The result is:

```text
[Amit, Priya, Neha]
```

Elements after the insertion position need to be shifted.

### addElement()

Vector also has a legacy method called addElement():

```java
names.addElement("Rahul");
```

It is functionally similar to adding an element at the end.

In modern code, the List API method add() is generally preferred because it works through the standard Collections Framework interface.

### addAll()

You can add all elements from another collection:

```java
List<String> additionalNames = List.of("Karan", "Ravi");
names.addAll(additionalNames);
```

Vector therefore supports both its historical methods and the standard List methods.

sections.title: Accessing and Updating Elements
sections.content:
Vector supports indexed access because it implements List and RandomAccess.

Use get() to retrieve an element:

```java
Vector<String> names = new Vector<>();
names.add("Amit");
names.add("Neha");
names.add("Raj");

String name = names.get(1);
System.out.println(name);
```

Output:

```text
Neha
```

You can update an element with set():

```java
names.set(1, "Priya");
```

The Vector becomes:

```text
[Amit, Priya, Raj]
```

Vector also has the older elementAt() method:

```java
System.out.println(names.elementAt(1));
```

Modern code will usually use get() because it is part of the List interface.

The key difference is:

```text
get(index)
    -> reads an element

set(index, value)
    -> replaces an element

add(index, value)
    -> inserts a new element
```

Both get() and set() provide direct indexed access to the underlying array.

sections.title: Removing Elements from Vector
Vector Synchronization and Thread Safety
Vector vs ArrayList
sections.content:
Vector and ArrayList are both dynamic-array implementations of List, but there are important differences.

```text
ArrayList
    -> Dynamic array
    -> Not synchronized by default
    -> Usually preferred for non-concurrent use

Vector
    -> Dynamic array
    -> Legacy synchronized methods
    -> Generally has more synchronization overhead
```

Both support:

- Insertion order
- Duplicate elements
- Null elements
- Indexed access
- Dynamic growth

Example:

```java
List<String> list1 = new ArrayList<>();
List<String> list2 = new Vector<>();
```

For a single-threaded application, ArrayList is usually the more natural choice because it avoids Vector's synchronization overhead.

If multiple threads need to share a list, simply choosing Vector should not automatically be treated as the best solution. Modern concurrent collection options can provide behavior better suited to the specific workload.

A strong interview answer should explain the design trade-off rather than saying only that Vector is "thread-safe" and ArrayList is "not thread-safe."

sections.title: Vector vs LinkedList
sections.content:
Vector and LinkedList both implement List, but their internal data structures are different.

```text
Vector
   -> Dynamically resized array
   -> Fast indexed access
   -> Middle insertion/removal requires shifting

LinkedList
   -> Doubly linked nodes
   -> Indexed access requires traversal
   -> Insertion/removal can be efficient when the relevant position/node is already known
```

For example, this operation is typically efficient with Vector:

```java
String value = vector.get(500);
```

because indexed access can use the backing array.

With LinkedList, finding index 500 requires traversing the linked structure.

However, this does not mean LinkedList is automatically faster for insertions and removals. The cost of finding the position must also be considered.

The correct implementation depends on how the collection is accessed and modified in the application.

sections.title: Vector Performance
sections.content:
Because Vector uses a dynamically resized array, its typical performance characteristics are similar to ArrayList for basic list operations, with synchronization overhead for its synchronized methods.

Typical complexity is:

```text
Operation                  Typical Complexity
------------------------------------------------
get(index)                 O(1)
set(index, value)          O(1)
add(value) at end          O(1) amortized
add(index, value)          O(n)
remove(index)              O(n)
remove(object)             O(n)
contains(object)           O(n)
indexOf(object)             O(n)
```

Why is get() O(1)?

The backing array allows direct access by index.

Why are middle insertions O(n)?

Elements after the insertion point generally have to be shifted.

Why is append O(1) amortized?

Most additions do not require resizing. Occasionally, the internal array must grow and elements must be copied, which takes O(n). Spread across many additions, the amortized cost remains constant.

sections.title: Legacy Methods in Vector
Vector Capacity Management Methods
sections.content:
Vector provides several methods for managing its internal capacity.

### capacity()

Returns the current capacity:

```java
Vector<Integer> numbers = new Vector<>(10);
System.out.println(numbers.capacity());
```

### ensureCapacity()

Ensures that the Vector can hold at least the specified number of elements without requiring immediate growth:

```java
numbers.ensureCapacity(1000);
```

### trimToSize()

Reduces the capacity to the current size:

```java
numbers.trimToSize();
```

For example:

```text
Before trim:
Size = 5
Capacity = 20

After trimToSize():
Size = 5
Capacity = 5
```

These methods are useful when capacity management matters, although they are not needed in most everyday application code.

The distinction between size and capacity is a common interview topic for Vector and ArrayList.

sections.title: Vector and Null Values
When Should You Use Vector?
sections.content:
Vector is mainly encountered in older Java applications, libraries, and legacy codebases.

For example, you may encounter code like:

```java
Vector<String> values = new Vector<>();
```

when maintaining an older application.

For new development, the decision should be based on the required behavior rather than simply choosing Vector because it is synchronized.

A simplified decision guide is:

```text
Need a general-purpose dynamic List
        -> ArrayList is often appropriate

Need specific concurrent access behavior
        -> Consider java.util.concurrent collections

Maintaining existing legacy code using Vector
        -> Vector may be retained when its behavior is required
```

Vector is therefore important to understand for Java interviews even though it is less common as the default choice in modern application development.

Knowing why it was historically used and how it differs from modern collection choices is more useful than simply memorizing its methods.

topics.shortDescription: Understand Java Vector, its dynamic-array implementation, synchronization, capacity management, legacy methods, and differences from ArrayList.

topics.title: Generics
topics.description: Learn Java Generics, including generic classes, methods, interfaces, bounded types, wildcards, type safety, type erasure, and practical usage with collections.

sections.title: What Are Generics in Java?
sections.content:
Generics allow you to write classes, interfaces, and methods that work with different types while still providing compile-time type safety.

Before generics were introduced, collections commonly stored values as Object:

```java
List names = new ArrayList();
names.add("Amit");
names.add("Neha");

String name = (String) names.get(0);
```

The developer had to cast the returned Object to the expected type. If an incorrect type was inserted, the problem might not be discovered until runtime.

Generics allow the type to be specified when the collection is declared:

```java
List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();

names.add("Amit");
names.add("Neha");
```

Now the compiler knows that this list is supposed to contain String values.

```java
names.add(100); // Compile-time error
```

The basic idea is:

```text
Without Generics
Collection -> Object -> Cast -> Actual Type

With Generics
Collection<String> -> String
```

Generics are one of the most important features used throughout the Java Collections Framework and modern Java application code.

sections.title: Why Do We Need Generics?
Generic Class
Generic Type Parameters
sections.content:
Java developers commonly use single uppercase letters for generic type parameters. These are naming conventions rather than special keywords.

Common names include:

```text
T -> Type
E -> Element
K -> Key
V -> Value
N -> Number
R -> Result
```

For example, Collection uses E conceptually to represent its element type:

```java
interface Collection<E> {
    boolean add(E e);
}
```

Map commonly uses K and V:

```java
Map<K, V>
```

For example:

```java
Map<Integer, String> employees = new HashMap<>();
```

Here:

```text
K = Integer
V = String
```

The letters themselves have no special meaning to the Java compiler. You could technically write:

```java
class Box<MyType> {
    private MyType value;
}
```

but conventional names make generic code much easier to understand.

sections.title: Generic Methods
Multiple Type Parameters
Generic Interfaces
Bounded Type Parameters
sections.content:
Sometimes you do not want a generic type to accept every possible class. You can restrict the allowed types using bounds.

For example:

```java
public static <T extends Number> double square(T value) {
    return value.doubleValue() * value.doubleValue();
}
```

Here T must be Number or a subclass of Number.

Valid calls include:

```java
square(10);
square(10.5);
square(100L);
```

A String would not be accepted:

```java
square("Hello"); // Compile-time error
```

The syntax is:

```java
<T extends SomeType>
```

The bound can also be an interface:

```java
<T extends Comparable<T>>
```

Multiple bounds are possible, with at most one class bound and any additional bounds being interfaces:

```java
<T extends Number & Comparable<T>>
```

Bounds are useful when the generic algorithm needs capabilities provided by a particular superclass or interface.

sections.title: Upper-Bounded Wildcard
Lower-Bounded Wildcard
sections.content:
A lower-bounded wildcard uses super:

```java
List<? super Integer>
```

It means the list is of Integer or one of Integer's supertypes.

For example:

```java
List<Number> numbers = new ArrayList<>();
List<Object> objects = new ArrayList<>();
```

Both can be used where List<? super Integer> is expected.

You can safely add an Integer:

```java
public static void addNumbers(List<? super Integer> list) {
    list.add(10);
    list.add(20);
}
```

The compiler knows that Integer can be stored safely because the destination is guaranteed to accept Integer.

However, when reading from a List<? super Integer>, the safe type you can assume is Object:

```java
List<? super Integer> values = new ArrayList<Number>();
values.add(10);

Object value = values.get(0);
```

A useful rule is:

```text
? super T
    -> consumer of T
    -> generally add T values to it
```

This leads to the commonly used PECS rule:

```text
Producer Extends
Consumer Super
```

sections.title: Unbounded Wildcard
sections.content:
An unbounded wildcard is written as:

```java
?
```

For example:

```java
List<?> values
```

It means a List of some unknown type.

You can use it when the method does not need to know the exact element type.

```java
public static void printList(List<?> list) {
    for (Object value : list) {
        System.out.println(value);
    }
}
```

This method can accept:

```java
printList(List.of("A", "B"));
printList(List.of(10, 20));
printList(List.of(10.5, 20.5));
```

You generally cannot add arbitrary values to a List<?> because the compiler does not know its actual element type.

```java
List<?> values = new ArrayList<String>();
// values.add("Hello"); // Compile-time error
```

The main difference is:

```text
List<T>
    -> exact type T is known

List<?>
    -> some type exists, but the exact type is unknown

List<? extends T>
    -> unknown subtype of T

List<? super T>
    -> unknown supertype of T
```

sections.title: PECS Principle
Type Erasure
sections.content:
Java generics are implemented using type erasure. Generic type information is primarily used by the compiler for type checking and is not generally retained as a concrete generic type parameter at runtime.

For example:

```java
List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();
```

The compiler checks that Strings are used correctly. At runtime, the JVM generally works with the raw collection representation rather than retaining String as a generic runtime type argument.

Conceptually:

```text
Source code
List<String>
     |
     | Compile-time type checking
     v
Bytecode/runtime representation
List
```

Because of type erasure, there are several restrictions.

For example, you cannot directly create an array of a type parameter:

```java
class Box<T> {
    // T[] values = new T[10]; // Compile-time error
}
```

You also cannot use a type parameter directly with instanceof:

```java
// if (value instanceof T) { } // Not allowed
```

Another important consequence is that generic type arguments are generally not available through ordinary runtime reflection in the same way as normal class information.

Type erasure allows generic Java code to remain compatible with much older Java bytecode and APIs while providing stronger compile-time type checking.

sections.title: Raw Types
sections.content:
A raw type is the use of a generic class or interface without specifying its type parameter.

For example:

```java
List names = new ArrayList();
```

This was common in Java code written before generics were introduced.

Raw types remove much of the compile-time type safety provided by generics:

```java
List names = new ArrayList();

names.add("Amit");
names.add(100);
```

The list can now contain unrelated types.

When reading values, casts may be required:

```java
String name = (String) names.get(0);
```

And this can fail at runtime:

```java
String value = (String) names.get(1);
```

because the actual object is an Integer.

Prefer parameterized types:

```java
List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();
```

Raw types are mainly encountered when maintaining legacy code or interacting with older APIs. Modern code should generally avoid them unless there is a specific compatibility reason.

sections.title: Generic Type Inference and the Diamond Operator
Generics and Primitive Types
sections.content:
Java generics work with reference types, not primitive types.

This is invalid:

```java
List<int> numbers = new ArrayList<>(); // Compile-time error
```

Use the corresponding wrapper type instead:

```java
List<Integer> numbers = new ArrayList<>();
numbers.add(10);
```

Java automatically converts the primitive int to Integer through autoboxing:

```text
int
 |
 | autoboxing
 v
Integer
```

When an Integer is used where an int is expected, Java can perform unboxing:

```text
Integer
 |
 | unboxing
 v
int
```

Example:

```java
List<Integer> numbers = new ArrayList<>();
numbers.add(10);

int value = numbers.get(0);
```

This works because the Integer returned from the list is automatically unboxed to int.

The same principle applies to other primitive wrapper types such as Long, Double, Boolean, Character, and Short.

sections.title: Generic Invariance
sections.content:
A common source of confusion is that generic types in Java are invariant.

Even though Integer extends Number, this does not mean:

```java
List<Integer> is a List<Number>
```

The following is therefore invalid:

```java
List<Integer> integers = new ArrayList<>();
// List<Number> numbers = integers; // Compile-time error
```

Why does Java prevent this?

Suppose it were allowed:

```java
List<Number> numbers = integers;
numbers.add(10.5); // Double
```

Then the original List<Integer> would contain a Double, violating its type guarantee.

Java avoids this problem by making generic types invariant.

When you need to express a relationship between generic types, wildcards can be used:

```java
List<? extends Number> numbers = integers;
```

Now the list can be viewed as a producer of Number values without allowing arbitrary Number subtypes to be inserted.

This is a very common interview question because it tests whether you understand the difference between normal inheritance and generic type relationships.

sections.title: Generic Constructors
Generic Methods with Multiple Bounds
sections.content:
A generic type parameter can have multiple bounds.

For example:

```java
public static <T extends Number & Comparable<T>> T max(T a, T b) {
    return a.compareTo(b) >= 0 ? a : b;
}
```

Here T must satisfy both requirements:

```text
T extends Number
        AND
T implements Comparable<T>
```

This allows the method to use methods from both Number and Comparable.

A class bound, if present, must appear first:

```java
<T extends SomeClass & InterfaceA & InterfaceB>
```

You cannot have two class bounds because Java classes support single inheritance.

Multiple interface bounds are allowed.

Bounds are particularly useful when a generic algorithm needs a specific set of capabilities rather than merely accepting every possible object.

sections.title: Common Mistakes with Generics
sections.content:
There are several mistakes developers commonly make when learning generics.

### Using raw types

Avoid:

```java
List list = new ArrayList();
```

Prefer:

```java
List<String> list = new ArrayList<>();
```

### Thinking List<Integer> is a List<Number>

Generic types are invariant.

```java
List<Integer> integers = new ArrayList<>();
// List<Number> numbers = integers; // Invalid
```

### Confusing extends with inheritance assignment

```java
List<? extends Number> numbers = new ArrayList<Integer>();
```

This does not mean that you can add arbitrary Number values to the list.

### Forgetting primitive types cannot be generic arguments

Use:

```java
List<Integer>
```

not:

```java
List<int>
```

### Assuming generics provide runtime type information

Generic type arguments are primarily a compile-time feature because of type erasure.

### Overusing wildcards

Wildcards are useful when type flexibility is needed, but they can make APIs harder to understand if used without a clear reason.

A good generic API should express the actual type relationship that the caller and implementation need.
