topics.title: Iterator
topics.description: Learn how Java Iterator works, including traversal, safe removal, fail-fast behavior, ListIterator, and common interview scenarios.

sections.title: What Is Iterator?
sections.content:
Iterator is an interface in the Java Collections Framework used to traverse elements of a collection one by one.

It belongs to the java.util package:

```java
import java.util.Iterator;
```

An Iterator provides a standard way to move through a collection without exposing how the collection stores its elements internally.

For example:

```java
List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();
names.add("Amit");
names.add("Neha");
names.add("Rahul");

Iterator<String> iterator = names.iterator();

while (iterator.hasNext()) {
    String name = iterator.next();
    System.out.println(name);
}
```

Output:

```text
Amit
Neha
Rahul
```

The basic idea is:

```text
Collection
    |
    | iterator()
    v
 Iterator
    |
    +--> hasNext()
    +--> next()
    +--> remove()
```

Iterator is useful because the same traversal API can be used with many different Collection implementations such as ArrayList, LinkedList, HashSet, and TreeSet.

sections.title: Why Use Iterator?
sections.content:
Different collections use different internal data structures. ArrayList uses a dynamic array, HashSet uses hash-based storage, and TreeSet uses a tree-based structure. You do not need to know those internal details just to traverse their elements.

Iterator provides a common traversal mechanism.

For example, the same pattern works with different collections:

```java
List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();
Set<String> uniqueNames = new HashSet<>();
```

Both provide an iterator:

```java
Iterator<String> iterator = names.iterator();
Iterator<String> setIterator = uniqueNames.iterator();
```

This provides abstraction between the collection and the code that consumes its elements.

Iterator is particularly useful when you need to remove elements during traversal. A normal enhanced for loop does not provide a direct way to safely perform structural removal from the underlying collection during the loop.

Instead of directly modifying the collection while iterating, you can use Iterator.remove().

sections.title: Important Iterator Methods
sections.content:
The Iterator interface provides three main methods that are commonly discussed.

### hasNext()

Checks whether another element is available.

```java
if (iterator.hasNext()) {
    System.out.println("More elements available");
}
```

It returns true if another element can be returned by next().

### next()

Returns the next element and moves the iterator's position forward.

```java
String name = iterator.next();
```

If there is no next element, next() throws NoSuchElementException.

### remove()

Removes from the underlying collection the last element returned by next().

```java
iterator.remove();
```

A typical iteration looks like:

```java
Iterator<String> iterator = names.iterator();

while (iterator.hasNext()) {
    String name = iterator.next();
    System.out.println(name);
}
```

The sequence is:

```text
hasNext()
   |
   v
 next()
   |
   v
 process element
   |
   v
hasNext()
   |
   v
 next()
```

The iterator maintains its own traversal position.

sections.title: Basic Iterator Example
Iterator and Safe Removal
Iterator.remove() Rules
sections.content:
Iterator.remove() has an important contract that is frequently asked about in interviews.

After creating an iterator, you must call next() before calling remove().

This is invalid:

```java
Iterator<String> iterator = names.iterator();
iterator.remove();
```

It results in IllegalStateException because no element has been returned by next().

A valid sequence is:

```java
String name = iterator.next();
iterator.remove();
```

After removing that element, calling remove() again without another next() is also invalid:

```java
iterator.next();
iterator.remove();
iterator.remove(); // IllegalStateException
```

The basic rule is:

```text
next()
  -> remove()       valid

next()
  -> remove()
  -> remove()       invalid

remove()            invalid
```

The iterator removes the last element returned by next(). This makes it possible to remove elements during traversal without directly modifying the collection through a separate reference.

sections.title: Fail-Fast Iterator
Iterator with Set
Iterator and Generics
sections.content:
Iterator works well with Java Generics because the element type can be specified explicitly.

For example:

```java
List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();

Iterator<String> iterator = names.iterator();
```

The compiler knows that next() returns String:

```java
String name = iterator.next();
```

Without generics:

```java
Iterator iterator = names.iterator();
Object value = iterator.next();
```

You may then need to cast:

```java
String name = (String) value;
```

Using generics therefore provides compile-time type safety and removes unnecessary casting.

The relationship is:

```text
Collection<String>
       |
       | iterator()
       v
Iterator<String>
       |
       | next()
       v
    String
```

This is one of the reasons Iterator is commonly used together with parameterized collections.

sections.title: Iterator vs Enhanced For Loop
Iterator vs ListIterator
ListIterator Additional Operations
Iterator and ConcurrentModificationException
Iterator and Multithreading
sections.content:
Iterator itself does not make a collection thread-safe.

For example, using an Iterator on an ArrayList while another thread modifies the same ArrayList can result in ConcurrentModificationException or other concurrency-related problems depending on the situation.

```java
List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();
Iterator<String> iterator = names.iterator();
```

The Iterator should not be treated as a synchronization mechanism.

If multiple threads access and modify shared collection data, choose an appropriate concurrency strategy. Depending on the use case, this could involve synchronized access, concurrent collections, immutable data, or other synchronization techniques.

For example, CopyOnWriteArrayList provides a different iterator behavior designed for specific read-heavy concurrent workloads.

The important distinction is:

```text
Iterator
    -> traversal mechanism

Synchronization
    -> concurrency control

Thread-safe collection
    -> collection designed/used with appropriate concurrency guarantees
```

These are separate concepts and should not be confused during interviews.

sections.title: Iterator with Map
Iterator vs Enumeration
sections.content:
Enumeration is an older Java interface that was mainly used with legacy collection classes such as Vector and Hashtable.

Iterator is the modern replacement for most ordinary traversal needs.

Enumeration provides methods such as:

```java
hasMoreElements()
nextElement()
```

Iterator provides:

```java
hasNext()
next()
remove()
```

A simplified comparison is:

```text
Enumeration
- Legacy API
- Mainly associated with older classes
- Cannot remove elements through the traversal interface

Iterator
- Part of Collections Framework
- Works with modern collections
- Supports remove()
```

Example of Enumeration:

```java
Vector<String> names = new Vector<>();
names.add("Amit");
names.add("Neha");

Enumeration<String> enumeration = names.elements();

while (enumeration.hasMoreElements()) {
    System.out.println(enumeration.nextElement());
}
```

You may encounter Enumeration when maintaining older Java code, but Iterator is generally the standard choice for collection traversal.

topics.title: Comparable
topics.description: Learn Java's Comparable interface, natural ordering, compareTo(), sorting custom objects, comparison rules, and common interview scenarios.

sections.title: What Is Comparable?
Why Do We Need Comparable?
compareTo() Method
sections.content:
The compareTo() method determines the relative ordering between two objects.

Its result is an int.

The important contract is:

```text
compareTo(other) < 0
    -> current object comes before other

compareTo(other) == 0
    -> objects are considered equal in ordering

compareTo(other) > 0
    -> current object comes after other
```

For example:

```java
class Employee implements Comparable<Employee> {
    private int salary;

    @Override
    public int compareTo(Employee other) {
        return Integer.compare(this.salary, other.salary);
    }
}
```

Suppose:

```text
Employee A salary = 50000
Employee B salary = 70000
```

Then:

```java
A.compareTo(B)
```

returns a negative value.

And:

```java
B.compareTo(A)
```

returns a positive value.

If both salaries are equal:

```java
A.compareTo(B)
```

returns 0.

The exact negative or positive number is normally not important. The sign of the result is what determines the ordering.

sections.title: Implementing Comparable with Custom Objects
Comparable with Collections.sort()
Natural Ordering
sections.content:
Natural ordering means the default ordering defined by a class.

Examples include:

```text
Integer
    -> numerical order

String
    -> lexicographical order

LocalDate
    -> chronological order
```

For a custom class, you define the natural ordering by implementing Comparable.

Example:

```java
class Product implements Comparable<Product> {
    private double price;

    @Override
    public int compareTo(Product other) {
        return Double.compare(this.price, other.price);
    }
}
```

Now Product objects have a natural ordering based on price.

The important design question is: what ordering should represent the class's default meaning?

If a class has several equally reasonable ways to sort its objects, Comparable may not be the best place to encode all of them. One natural ordering can be defined with Comparable, while alternative orderings can be provided using Comparator.

For example:

```text
Employee natural ordering -> salary
Alternative ordering      -> name
Alternative ordering      -> id
```

This is one of the main reasons Comparable and Comparator are often discussed together.

sections.title: Comparable vs Comparator
sections.content:
Comparable and Comparator both help Java determine how objects should be ordered, but they are designed for different purposes.

### Comparable

The class itself defines its natural ordering:

```java
class Employee implements Comparable<Employee> {

    @Override
    public int compareTo(Employee other) {
        return Double.compare(this.salary, other.salary);
    }
}
```

### Comparator

The ordering is defined separately from the class:

```java
Comparator<Employee> byName =
        Comparator.comparing(Employee::getName);
```

Then:

```java
employees.sort(byName);
```

A simplified comparison is:

```text
Comparable
    -> defined inside the class
    -> one natural ordering
    -> compareTo()

Comparator
    -> defined separately
    -> multiple possible orderings
    -> compare()
```

For example, Employee could have salary as its natural ordering while separate Comparators sort by name, id, or department.

This makes Comparator especially useful when the class should not be modified or when an application needs several different sorting strategies.

sections.title: Ascending and Descending Order
Comparing Strings with Comparable
Comparable and TreeSet
Comparable and TreeMap
Comparable Contract
sections.content:
The Comparable interface has an important contract. Understanding it is more useful than memorizing only the method signature.

For objects x and y:

```text
sgn(x.compareTo(y)) == -sgn(y.compareTo(x))
```

In simpler terms, if x comes before y, y should come after x.

The ordering should also be transitive. If:

```text
A < B
B < C
```

then the comparison should consistently indicate:

```text
A < C
```

Another important property is consistency of comparison results.

If x.compareTo(y) returns 0, then x and y are considered equal in terms of ordering.

The Comparable documentation also discusses consistency with equals. It is strongly recommended that natural ordering be consistent with equals when possible, although it is not an absolute requirement of the Comparable interface.

A poorly implemented compareTo() can cause incorrect sorting or surprising behavior in sorted collections such as TreeSet and TreeMap.

sections.title: Comparable and equals()
sections.content:
Comparable and equals() serve different purposes.

equals() answers whether two objects are equal according to the class's equality definition.

compareTo() determines their relative ordering.

For example:

```java
@Override
public boolean equals(Object obj) {
    // equality logic
}

@Override
public int compareTo(Employee other) {
    return Integer.compare(this.id, other.id);
}
```

Ideally, if:

```java
x.compareTo(y) == 0
```

then:

```java
x.equals(y)
```

should also be true.

But Java does not require every Comparable implementation to have a natural ordering consistent with equals.

A classic example is BigDecimal, where compareTo() and equals() use different notions of equality:

```java
new BigDecimal("1.0").compareTo(new BigDecimal("1.00")) == 0
```

while their equals() result is false because scale is considered by BigDecimal.equals().

This distinction becomes important with TreeSet and TreeMap because sorted collections use comparison to determine element/key equivalence.

sections.title: Using Comparator.comparing with Comparable Classes
Avoiding Arithmetic Comparison Bugs
sections.content:
A common mistake when implementing compareTo() is comparing numbers using subtraction.

For example:

```java
@Override
public int compareTo(Employee other) {
    return this.id - other.id;
}
```

This looks simple, but integer subtraction can overflow.

For example, if one value is very large and the other is negative, the subtraction may produce an incorrect sign after overflow.

Prefer the built-in comparison methods:

```java
return Integer.compare(this.id, other.id);
```

For long values:

```java
return Long.compare(this.id, other.id);
```

For double values:

```java
return Double.compare(this.salary, other.salary);
```

For strings:

```java
return this.name.compareTo(other.name);
```

For nullable values, use appropriate Comparator utilities when null handling is required.

The general principle is to make compareTo() express the intended ordering clearly and safely.

sections.title: Multiple Fields in compareTo()
sections.content:
Sometimes an object needs to be ordered using more than one field.

For example, suppose employees should be sorted by department and then by name.

Modern Java code can express this using Comparator composition:

```java
Comparator<Employee> comparator =
        Comparator.comparing(Employee::getDepartment)
                  .thenComparing(Employee::getName);
```

If the same ordering truly represents the class's natural ordering, the class can use a similar comparison strategy inside compareTo(), for example:

```java
@Override
public int compareTo(Employee other) {
    int result = this.department.compareTo(other.department);

    if (result != 0) {
        return result;
    }

    return this.name.compareTo(other.name);
}
```

The comparison works in stages:

```text
Compare department
       |
       +-- Different -> return result
       |
       +-- Same
             |
             v
        Compare name
```

When building a natural ordering, make sure the comparison fields provide a stable and logically consistent ordering.

sections.title: Comparable and Null Values
Comparable with Streams
sections.content:
Comparable can also be used when sorting objects through Java Streams.

For example:

```java
List<Employee> sorted = employees.stream()
        .sorted()
        .toList();
```

The no-argument sorted() operation uses the elements' natural ordering.

Therefore, Employee must implement Comparable<Employee> for this form:

```java
class Employee implements Comparable<Employee> {
    @Override
    public int compareTo(Employee other) {
        return Integer.compare(this.id, other.id);
    }
}
```

You can also provide a Comparator to use a different ordering:

```java
List<Employee> sorted = employees.stream()
        .sorted(Comparator.comparing(Employee::getName))
        .toList();
```

The distinction is:

```text
sorted()
    -> natural ordering
    -> Comparable

sorted(comparator)
    -> supplied ordering
    -> Comparator
```

This is useful in modern Java applications where collection processing and sorting are often performed through streams.

topics.title: TreeSet
topics.description: TreeSet is a sorted Set implementation in Java that stores unique elements in a navigable, ordered structure backed by a Red-Black tree. This topic explains how TreeSet works, how ordering and uniqueness are determined, important methods, custom objects, Comparable and Comparator, performance, null handling, and common interview scenarios.

sections.title: What is TreeSet?
Why Use TreeSet?
TreeSet Class Hierarchy
sections.content:
TreeSet implements the NavigableSet interface and therefore also inherits behavior from SortedSet and Set.

The simplified hierarchy is:

```text
Iterable
   |
Collection
   |
Set
   |
SortedSet
   |
NavigableSet
   |
TreeSet
```

TreeSet is also backed internally by a TreeMap. The TreeMap uses a Red-Black tree to maintain its keys in sorted order.

This internal structure is the main reason TreeSet can efficiently perform ordered and navigation operations.

sections.title: How TreeSet Maintains Sorted Order
sections.content:
TreeSet does not sort the complete collection every time you add an element. Internally, it maintains a balanced search tree and places each new element at the appropriate position.

Conceptually, the structure looks like this:

```text
             30
           /    \
         20      50
        /  \    /  \
      10   25  40   60
```

The actual Red-Black tree structure is implementation-specific, but the important idea is that the tree remains balanced enough to provide logarithmic-time operations.

Because the elements are kept ordered as they are inserted, iteration produces sorted values without requiring an additional sorting operation.

sections.title: TreeSet and Duplicate Elements
Natural Ordering with Comparable
TreeSet with Comparator
TreeSet with Custom Objects
Important TreeSet Navigation Methods
First and Last Elements
Range Operations
Inclusive and Exclusive Range Boundaries
Descending Order and descendingSet()
TreeSet and Null Values
TreeSet and equals()
sections.content:
A common interview point is that TreeSet does not use equals() as the primary mechanism for deciding whether two elements are duplicates. It uses compareTo() or Comparator.compare().

For example, suppose two Employee objects have different ids but the comparator compares only their department:

```java
Comparator<Employee> comparator =
    Comparator.comparing(Employee::getDepartment);
```

If two employees compare as 0, TreeSet can keep only one of them even though equals() may consider them different.

Therefore, the ordering used by a TreeSet should normally be consistent with equals when logical set behavior is expected.

This is one of the most important differences between a TreeSet and a HashSet.

sections.title: Time Complexity of TreeSet
sections.content:
Because TreeSet is based on a balanced tree, its basic search and update operations generally take O(log n) time.

Typical complexity:

```text
add()        -> O(log n)
remove()     -> O(log n)
contains()   -> O(log n)
first()      -> O(log n) or implementation-dependent constant-time path access
last()       -> O(log n) or implementation-dependent constant-time path access
lower()      -> O(log n)
floor()      -> O(log n)
higher()     -> O(log n)
ceiling()    -> O(log n)
```

Iteration over all elements is O(n).

This makes TreeSet a useful choice when ordered operations are needed and O(log n) updates are acceptable.

sections.title: TreeSet vs HashSet
sections.content:
Both TreeSet and HashSet store unique elements, but their internal behavior and guarantees are different.

```text
HashSet
- Hash-table based
- No sorted-order guarantee
- Average O(1) add/search/remove
- Useful for fast membership checks

TreeSet
- Red-Black tree based through TreeMap
- Sorted order
- O(log n) add/search/remove
- Supports range and navigation operations
```

Example use cases:

Use HashSet when you mainly need to answer: 'Have I already seen this value?'

Use TreeSet when you need to answer questions such as: 'What is the smallest value greater than X?' or 'Give me all values between X and Y.'

sections.title: TreeSet vs TreeMap
TreeSet with Streams
sections.content:
TreeSet can be used together with the Stream API when you want to perform transformations while preserving or creating sorted unique data.

Example:

```java
List<Integer> numbers = List.of(40, 10, 30, 20, 10, 40);

TreeSet<Integer> result = numbers.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.toCollection(TreeSet::new));

System.out.println(result);
```

Output:

```text
[10, 20, 30, 40]
```

A TreeSet can also be created directly from another collection:

```java
TreeSet<Integer> numbers = new TreeSet<>(List.of(30, 10, 20, 10));
```

This is a convenient way to obtain unique sorted values.

sections.title: Thread Safety
sections.content:
TreeSet is not thread-safe. If multiple threads modify the same TreeSet concurrently, external synchronization or another concurrency strategy is required.

For example, synchronized access can be created with Collections.synchronizedSortedSet():

```java
SortedSet<Integer> numbers =
    Collections.synchronizedSortedSet(new TreeSet<>());
```

For concurrent applications where sorted and navigable access is required, ConcurrentSkipListSet is often considered instead.

```java
NavigableSet<Integer> numbers = new ConcurrentSkipListSet<>();
```

The choice depends on the application's concurrency requirements rather than simply replacing every TreeSet with a concurrent collection.

sections.title: Common TreeSet Mistakes
sections.content:
Some common mistakes when using TreeSet are:

1. Assuming TreeSet preserves insertion order. It does not; it maintains sorted order.
2. Adding incompatible element types when no suitable ordering exists.
3. Forgetting that compareTo() returning 0 can cause an element to be treated as a duplicate.
4. Writing a Comparator that is inconsistent with the application's equality semantics.
5. Assuming TreeSet operations are O(1), as they are generally O(log n).
6. Modifying a TreeSet while iterating without using a supported removal approach.
7. Using mutable fields involved in comparison and then changing those fields while the object is stored in the TreeSet.
8. Assuming TreeSet is thread-safe.

A particularly subtle bug occurs when a comparator compares only one field while the application expects objects with different values in that field to coexist.

topics.shortDescription: Learn how TreeSet stores unique elements in sorted order, how Comparable and Comparator control ordering, how navigation and range operations work, and when TreeSet is preferable to HashSet.

topics.title: HashSet
topics.description: HashSet is a Set implementation in Java used to store unique elements without maintaining a guaranteed iteration order. This topic explains how HashSet works internally, how hashing and equals() determine duplicates, collision handling, resizing, capacity and load factor, null handling, custom objects, performance, fail-fast iteration, thread safety, and common interview scenarios.

sections.title: What is HashSet?
Why Use HashSet?
HashSet Class Hierarchy
sections.content:
HashSet is part of the Java Collections Framework and implements the Set interface.

A simplified hierarchy is:

```text
Iterable
   |
Collection
   |
Set
   |
HashSet
```

HashSet extends AbstractSet, which provides common Set behavior.

```text
AbstractCollection
       |
   AbstractSet
       |
    HashSet
```

HashSet can therefore be used anywhere a Collection or Set is expected.

sections.title: How HashSet Works Internally
sections.content:
HashSet uses a HashMap internally. The elements stored in the HashSet are effectively stored as keys in the backing HashMap, while a shared dummy value is used as the corresponding map value.

Conceptually:

```text
HashSet
   |
   v
HashMap
   |
   +---- element A -> dummy value
   +---- element B -> dummy value
   +---- element C -> dummy value
```

When you call add(), HashSet delegates the underlying storage operation to the HashMap.

For example:

```java
HashSet<String> set = new HashSet<>();
set.add("Java");
```

Internally, the string "Java" is stored as a key in the backing HashMap.

This relationship is an important interview question because many HashSet behaviors are directly related to HashMap's hashing implementation.

sections.title: How Hashing Determines the Storage Location
sections.content:
When an element is added to a HashSet, Java obtains its hash value and uses it to determine where the element should be stored in the underlying hash table.

Conceptually:

```text
Object
  |
  v
hashCode()
  |
  v
hash value
  |
  v
bucket/index
```

For example:

```java
String value = "Java";
int hash = value.hashCode();

System.out.println(hash);
```

The exact internal index calculation is an implementation detail, but the important idea is that the hash value helps locate the appropriate bucket quickly.

A good hash distribution reduces collisions and helps maintain efficient average performance.

sections.title: hashCode() and equals() in HashSet
sections.content:
HashSet relies on both hashCode() and equals() when determining whether an element already exists.

The general process is:

```text
add(element)
     |
     v
calculate hash
     |
     v
find bucket
     |
     v
check existing entries
     |
     +---- hash differs -> different candidate
     |
     +---- same hash -> equals() check
                         |
                         +---- true  -> duplicate
                         +---- false -> new element
```

The equals() method is important because different objects can have the same hash code. A hash collision does not automatically mean that two objects are equal.

The contract requires that if two objects are equal according to equals(), they must return the same hashCode().

sections.title: Why hashCode() and equals() Must Be Consistent
What Happens During add()?
sections.content:
When add(element) is called, HashSet attempts to insert the element into its backing hash table.

A simplified flow is:

```text
set.add(element)
       |
       v
calculate hash
       |
       v
find bucket
       |
       v
bucket empty?
   /          \
 yes           no
  |             |
store       compare candidates
                |
          equals() comparison
             /       \
          equal     different
            |           |
        don't add    store element
```

The add() method returns true when the set changes and false when the element was already present.

```java
Set<String> languages = new HashSet<>();

System.out.println(languages.add("Java"));
System.out.println(languages.add("Java"));
```

Output:

```text
true
false
```

sections.title: Hash Collisions
sections.content:
A hash collision occurs when different objects produce the same hash value or are mapped to the same bucket.

For example, conceptually:

```text
Object A ---- hash ----> Bucket 5
Object B ---- hash ----> Bucket 5
Object C ---- hash ----> Bucket 2
```

A collision does not mean HashSet considers the objects duplicates. Java still uses equality comparison to distinguish objects that share a bucket.

Modern Java implementations of HashMap can convert a heavily populated bucket from a linked structure to a balanced tree structure under suitable conditions. This helps prevent poor performance when many keys collide.

The exact thresholds and implementation details are part of the JDK implementation and can change between versions.

sections.title: Initial Capacity and Load Factor
sections.content:
HashSet has an internal hash table whose capacity grows as more elements are inserted. Two important concepts are initial capacity and load factor.

The load factor controls how full the table can become before resizing is triggered. The commonly used default load factor is 0.75.

Conceptually:

```text
threshold = capacity × load factor
```

For example, with a capacity of 16 and a load factor of 0.75, the threshold is approximately 12 entries before a resize is triggered.

You can provide an initial capacity and load factor when creating a HashSet:

```java
Set<String> set = new HashSet<>(32, 0.75f);
```

Choosing a suitable initial capacity can reduce repeated resizing when the approximate number of elements is already known.

sections.title: Resizing and Rehashing
sections.content:
When the number of stored entries reaches the table's resize threshold, the underlying hash table grows. Existing entries must then be redistributed into the new table according to the new capacity.

Conceptually:

```text
Before resize

[0]  A
[1]
[2]  B
[3]  C

       resize
          |
          v

After resize

[0]
[1]  A
[2]
[3]  C
[4]  B
[5]
...
```

This operation can temporarily be more expensive than a normal insertion. However, resizing happens periodically, so HashSet operations are generally described as having average constant-time performance under good hashing behavior.

Providing a reasonable initial capacity can be useful when a large collection is expected.

sections.title: Time Complexity of HashSet
sections.content:
Under normal conditions with a good hash distribution, HashSet provides average O(1) time for basic operations.

Typical complexity:

```text
add()       -> O(1) average
contains()   -> O(1) average
remove()     -> O(1) average
```

Iteration is O(n) because every table position may need to be examined.

Worst-case behavior depends on collisions and the underlying implementation. Modern JDK implementations can treeify heavily populated buckets under certain conditions, improving worst-case behavior for suitable key types.

When discussing complexity in interviews, say 'average O(1)' for HashSet rather than claiming that every operation is always O(1).

sections.title: Does HashSet Maintain Insertion Order?
Can HashSet Store null?
HashSet with Custom Objects
Mutable Objects and HashSet
HashSet Iteration
Removing Elements Safely
HashSet vs LinkedHashSet
sections.content:
HashSet and LinkedHashSet both store unique elements using hashing, but they differ in iteration-order behavior.

```text
HashSet
- Unique elements
- No guaranteed iteration order
- Generally lower structural overhead

LinkedHashSet
- Unique elements
- Maintains insertion order
- Uses additional linked-list structure
```

Example:

```java
Set<String> hashSet = new HashSet<>();
Set<String> linkedSet = new LinkedHashSet<>();

hashSet.add("B");
hashSet.add("A");

linkedSet.add("B");
linkedSet.add("A");
```

Choose HashSet when ordering is irrelevant. Choose LinkedHashSet when predictable insertion-order iteration is required.

sections.title: HashSet vs TreeSet
sections.content:
HashSet and TreeSet both enforce uniqueness, but they are designed for different requirements.

```text
HashSet
- Hash-based
- No guaranteed sorted order
- Average O(1) basic operations
- Good for fast membership checks

TreeSet
- Tree-based
- Sorted order
- O(log n) basic operations
- Supports range and navigation operations
```

For example, if you only need to know whether an ID exists, HashSet is a natural fit.

If you need operations such as 'find the smallest value greater than X', TreeSet provides methods such as higher() and ceiling() directly.

sections.title: HashSet vs List
Thread Safety
sections.content:
HashSet is not thread-safe. Multiple threads should not concurrently modify the same HashSet without appropriate synchronization.

If synchronized access is sufficient, a synchronized wrapper can be used:

```java
Set<String> names =
    Collections.synchronizedSet(new HashSet<>());
```

For concurrent applications, ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet() provides a concurrent Set implementation:

```java
Set<String> names = ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet();
```

The appropriate choice depends on whether the application needs simple synchronization or highly concurrent access.

Wrapping a HashSet with synchronization does not automatically make every compound operation atomic. Multi-step operations may still require explicit synchronization.

sections.title: Common HashSet Mistakes
sections.content:
Common HashSet mistakes include:

1. Assuming HashSet preserves insertion order.
2. Assuming HashSet always provides O(1) performance regardless of hashing quality.
3. Overriding equals() without overriding hashCode().
4. Modifying fields used by equals() and hashCode() after insertion.
5. Expecting two objects with the same hashCode() to automatically be treated as duplicates.
6. Modifying the set directly while using an iterator.
7. Assuming HashSet is thread-safe.
8. Using HashSet when sorted or insertion-order traversal is actually required.
9. Writing poor hashCode() implementations that cause excessive collisions.
10. Depending on the current observed iteration order even though the API does not guarantee it.

topics.shortDescription: Learn how HashSet stores unique elements using hashing, how hashCode() and equals() work together, how collisions and resizing are handled, and when to choose HashSet over List, LinkedHashSet, or TreeSet.

topics.title: HashMap
topics.description: HashMap is a hash-based Map implementation in Java that stores key-value pairs and provides efficient average-time lookup, insertion, and removal. This topic explains how HashMap works internally, hashing, buckets, collisions, equals() and hashCode(), resizing, load factor, treeification, null keys, custom objects, iteration, fail-fast behavior, thread safety, and practical interview scenarios.

sections.title: What is HashMap?
Why Use HashMap?
HashMap Class Hierarchy
sections.content:
HashMap implements the Map interface and extends AbstractMap.

A simplified hierarchy is:

```text
Map
 |
AbstractMap
 |
HashMap
```

HashMap is not a subtype of Collection because Map represents a separate collection concept based on key-value mappings.

HashMap also implements Serializable and Cloneable.

Other commonly used Map implementations include:

```text
Map
├── HashMap
├── LinkedHashMap
├── TreeMap
├── Hashtable
└── ConcurrentHashMap
```

Each implementation has different ordering, concurrency, and performance characteristics.

sections.title: How HashMap Works Internally
sections.content:
HashMap uses a hash table internally. In modern Java implementations, the table is an array of buckets. Each bucket can contain one or more entries.

Conceptually:

```text
HashMap
   |
   v
Hash table
   |
   +---- Bucket 0
   +---- Bucket 1 -> Entry
   +---- Bucket 2
   +---- Bucket 3 -> Entry -> Entry
   +---- Bucket 4
   +---- ...
```

Each entry contains information similar to:

```text
hash
key
value
next
```

The exact internal implementation is JDK-specific, but the core idea is that the key's hash helps locate a bucket where the mapping is stored.

HashMap therefore avoids scanning every key for a normal lookup.

sections.title: What Happens During put()?
sections.content:
When you call put(key, value), HashMap calculates a hash for the key and uses that information to identify the bucket where the mapping belongs.

A simplified flow is:

```text
put(key, value)
       |
       v
calculate key hash
       |
       v
find bucket
       |
       v
bucket empty?
   /          \
 yes           no
  |             |
insert       compare keys
                |
           equals() check
             /       \
          equal     different
            |           |
       replace value   handle collision
```

If an existing key is found, its value is replaced and the old value is returned by put(). If no matching key exists, a new mapping is added.

sections.title: What Happens During get()?
sections.content:
The get() operation uses the key to locate the appropriate bucket and then searches the entries in that bucket for a matching key.

Conceptually:

```text
get(key)
   |
   v
hash key
   |
   v
find bucket
   |
   v
compare candidate keys
   |
   v
matching key?
  /       \
 yes       no
 |          |
value     null
```

Example:

```java
Map<String, Integer> scores = new HashMap<>();
scores.put("Amit", 90);
scores.put("Neha", 95);

Integer score = scores.get("Neha");
System.out.println(score);
```

Output:

```text
95
```

Under normal conditions, lookup is O(1) on average.

sections.title: hashCode() in HashMap
sections.content:
HashMap uses the key's hashCode() as part of determining where the key-value mapping should be stored.

Example:

```java
String key = "Java";

System.out.println(key.hashCode());
```

HashMap applies its internal hash-processing logic before using the result to locate a table bucket.

The important point is that hashCode() does not directly identify a unique bucket for every object. Different keys can produce the same hash value or end up in the same bucket.

This is why HashMap also needs equals() to determine whether two keys actually represent the same key.

sections.title: equals() and hashCode() in HashMap
Hash Collisions
sections.content:
A hash collision occurs when different keys produce the same hash value or are assigned to the same bucket.

For example:

```text
Key A ----> Bucket 3
Key B ----> Bucket 3
Key C ----> Bucket 7
```

Key A and Key B can still be different keys. HashMap uses key comparison to distinguish them.

Older implementations primarily used linked structures for collisions. Modern Java implementations can convert a sufficiently large collision chain into a balanced tree under certain conditions.

This treeification helps prevent a large number of collisions from causing very slow lookup behavior.

The exact treeification thresholds and implementation details are JDK-specific and should not be treated as immutable API guarantees.

sections.title: Treeification in HashMap
sections.content:
In modern Java implementations, a heavily populated bucket can be converted from a linked structure into a Red-Black tree when certain implementation thresholds are reached and the table is sufficiently large.

Conceptually:

```text
Before:

Bucket
  |
  v
Entry -> Entry -> Entry -> Entry

After treeification:

       Entry
       /   \
    Entry  Entry
           /   \
        Entry  Entry
```

This can improve lookup behavior for heavily collided buckets.

However, you should not describe HashMap simply as 'a Red-Black tree.' HashMap is fundamentally a hash-table-based structure whose individual heavily populated buckets may be treeified in modern JDK implementations.

sections.title: Load Factor and Initial Capacity
sections.content:
HashMap has two important configuration concepts: initial capacity and load factor.

The load factor determines how full the hash table can become before resizing is triggered. The commonly used default load factor is 0.75.

Conceptually:

```text
threshold = capacity × loadFactor
```

For a capacity of 16 and a load factor of 0.75, the threshold is approximately 12 entries.

You can specify these values:

```java
Map<String, Integer> map =
    new HashMap<>(32, 0.75f);
```

A higher load factor can reduce memory usage but may increase collisions. A lower load factor generally provides more empty buckets but can use more memory.

sections.title: HashMap Resizing
sections.content:
When the number of entries reaches the resize threshold, HashMap increases the table capacity and redistributes the existing mappings across the new table.

Conceptually:

```text
Initial table

[0] -> A
[1]
[2] -> B
[3] -> C

       resize
          |
          v

Larger table

[0]
[1] -> A
[2]
[3] -> C
[4]
[5] -> B
...
```

Resizing is more expensive than a normal insertion because existing entries need to be processed. However, resizing does not happen on every insertion.

If the approximate number of entries is known in advance, choosing an appropriate initial capacity can reduce unnecessary resizing.

sections.title: HashMap Capacity and Power of Two
sections.content:
HashMap's internal table capacity is maintained as a power of two in standard OpenJDK implementations.

Examples include:

```text
16
32
64
128
256
...
```

This design works with the internal bucket-index calculation and allows efficient bitwise operations.

A common interview mistake is to assume that the capacity supplied to the constructor is always the exact initial table size. HashMap may internally round the requested capacity to an appropriate power-of-two capacity, and table allocation is also lazy in modern implementations.

The public API does not require developers to depend on these implementation details.

sections.title: Can HashMap Have a Null Key?
Duplicate Keys in HashMap
Important HashMap Methods
get() vs getOrDefault()
sections.content:
get() returns the mapped value or null when no mapping exists. getOrDefault() allows you to provide a fallback value.

Example:

```java
Map<String, Integer> scores = new HashMap<>();
scores.put("Amit", 90);

System.out.println(scores.get("Raj"));
System.out.println(scores.getOrDefault("Raj", 0));
```

Output:

```text
null
0
```

This is useful when a missing key should naturally map to a default value.

One subtle point is that HashMap permits null values, so get(key) returning null does not by itself prove that the key is absent. Use containsKey() when you need to distinguish 'no mapping' from 'mapping exists with null value.'

sections.title: computeIfAbsent()
merge() for Counting
Iterating Over HashMap
HashMap Views: keySet(), values(), and entrySet()
Fail-Fast Iterators
HashMap and Mutable Keys
sections.content:
A key used in a HashMap should generally be immutable with respect to the fields used by equals() and hashCode().

Suppose a key is inserted and then one of its equality-related fields changes. A later get() may fail because the key may now produce a different hash value and therefore be searched for in a different bucket.

Conceptually:

```text
Insert key
   |
   v
hash = H1
   |
   v
stored in bucket B1

Key is modified
   |
   v
hash = H2
   |
   v
lookup searches bucket B2
```

The original mapping may still physically exist in the table, but the lookup can no longer locate it using the modified key.

This is why immutable key classes such as String are excellent HashMap keys.

sections.title: HashMap Time Complexity
sections.content:
Under normal conditions with a good hash distribution, HashMap provides average O(1) time for basic key-based operations.

Typical complexity:

```text
put()       -> O(1) average
get()       -> O(1) average
remove()    -> O(1) average
containsKey -> O(1) average
```

Iteration through all mappings is O(n).

Worst-case behavior depends on collisions and the implementation. Modern JDK implementations can treeify heavily populated buckets under suitable conditions, which can improve lookup behavior in those buckets.

Resizing can temporarily require processing many existing entries, so O(1) should be understood as an average/amortized expectation rather than a guarantee for every individual operation.

sections.title: HashMap vs Hashtable
sections.content:
HashMap and Hashtable are both key-value data structures, but they have important differences.

```text
HashMap
- Not synchronized by default
- Allows one null key
- Allows null values
- Modern general-purpose choice

Hashtable
- Synchronized legacy implementation
- Does not allow null keys or null values
- Generally avoided in new code when modern alternatives are available
```

For concurrent applications, ConcurrentHashMap is usually more appropriate than using Hashtable merely because synchronization is required.

The choice should be based on the application's actual concurrency and API requirements.

sections.title: HashMap vs LinkedHashMap
sections.content:
LinkedHashMap extends HashMap behavior by maintaining a linked structure that provides predictable iteration order.

```text
HashMap
- Unique keys
- No guaranteed iteration order
- Hash-based lookup

LinkedHashMap
- Unique keys
- Predictable insertion-order iteration by default
- Can also be configured for access-order behavior
```

Example:

```java
Map<Integer, String> map = new LinkedHashMap<>();
map.put(3, "C");
map.put(1, "A");
map.put(2, "B");

System.out.println(map);
```

The entries iterate in their maintained linked order.

LinkedHashMap is often useful when you need HashMap-style lookup together with predictable iteration order, such as implementing certain cache or recently-used-entry patterns.

sections.title: HashMap vs TreeMap
sections.content:
HashMap and TreeMap both store key-value pairs but provide different ordering behavior.

```text
HashMap
- Hash-based
- No guaranteed key ordering
- Average O(1) basic operations
- Supports one null key

TreeMap
- Tree-based
- Keys maintained in sorted order
- O(log n) basic operations
- Supports navigable and range operations
```

Use HashMap when fast key-based lookup is the main requirement and key order does not matter.

Use TreeMap when sorted keys, range queries, or navigation operations are part of the requirement.

sections.title: HashMap vs ConcurrentHashMap
sections.content:
HashMap is not thread-safe, while ConcurrentHashMap is designed for concurrent access.

```text
HashMap
- No built-in thread safety
- Suitable for single-threaded or externally synchronized access

ConcurrentHashMap
- Designed for concurrent access
- Supports concurrent reads and updates
- Does not allow null keys or null values
```

For example:

```java
Map<String, Integer> counters = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

counters.merge("requests", 1, Integer::sum);
```

ConcurrentHashMap is generally a better choice when multiple threads need to update a shared map concurrently.

Simply wrapping a HashMap with synchronization can be appropriate for some workloads, but it has different concurrency characteristics from ConcurrentHashMap.

sections.title: Thread Safety of HashMap
sections.content:
HashMap is not thread-safe. Multiple threads should not concurrently modify a shared HashMap without appropriate synchronization.

For simple synchronized access, a synchronized wrapper can be used:

```java
Map<String, Integer> map =
    Collections.synchronizedMap(new HashMap<>());
```

For highly concurrent workloads, ConcurrentHashMap is usually a better fit:

```java
Map<String, Integer> map = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
```

Thread safety is not only about individual method calls. Compound operations such as 'check whether a key exists, then insert it' may require atomic map methods such as putIfAbsent() or computeIfAbsent(), depending on the requirement.
