topics.title: Executing SQL Query
topics.description: Learn how to execute SQL statements using JDBC, including Statement, PreparedStatement, CallableStatement, executeQuery(), executeUpdate(), execute(), parameter binding, batch operations, generated keys, transactions, and practical database access patterns.

sections.title: What Does Executing an SQL Query Mean?
sections.content:
Executing an SQL query in JDBC means sending an SQL statement from a Java application to the database through a JDBC driver and receiving the result or update count.

The basic flow is:

```text
Java Application
       |
       v
    JDBC API
       |
       v
Statement / PreparedStatement
       |
       v
 JDBC Driver
       |
       v
    Database
       |
       v
ResultSet / Update Count
```

JDBC provides different methods depending on whether the SQL returns rows, modifies data, or may produce different types of results.

sections.title: Steps to Execute SQL Using JDBC
Statement Interface
PreparedStatement Interface
executeQuery()
executeUpdate()
execute()
executeQuery vs executeUpdate vs execute
sections.content:
The three methods serve different purposes.

```text
executeQuery()
     |
     +--> ResultSet

executeUpdate()
     |
     +--> int update count

execute()
     |
     +--> boolean indicating first result type
```

Typical usage:

```text
SELECT             -> executeQuery()
INSERT             -> executeUpdate()
UPDATE             -> executeUpdate()
DELETE             -> executeUpdate()
DDL without rows   -> executeUpdate() commonly used
Mixed results      -> execute()
```

The exact behavior for unusual SQL depends on the JDBC specification, database, and driver, so the driver's documentation should be checked for database-specific cases.

sections.title: Executing a SELECT Query
Executing an INSERT Query
Executing an UPDATE Query
Executing a DELETE Query
Parameter Binding
Why PreparedStatement Is Safer
Reading ResultSet
Handling NULL Values
sections.content:
SQL NULL is different from Java null and requires some care when reading primitive values from ResultSet.

For example:

```java
int salary = rs.getInt("salary");
boolean wasNull = rs.wasNull();
```

If the database value is SQL NULL, getInt() returns the primitive default value 0, so wasNull() can be used to determine whether the retrieved value was actually SQL NULL.

For nullable numeric fields, wrapper types or getObject() with an appropriate Java type can sometimes make the distinction easier to represent in application code.

sections.title: Executing Batch SQL Operations
Generated Keys After INSERT
Executing SQL Inside a Transaction
CallableStatement for Stored Procedures
Executing DDL Statements
Executing Multiple Results
sections.content:
Some SQL operations or stored procedures can produce multiple results. JDBC provides methods such as getMoreResults() and getUpdateCount() to navigate through them.

Conceptually:

```text
execute()
   |
   v
First Result
   |
   v
getMoreResults()
   |
   v
Next Result
   |
   v
getMoreResults()
   |
   v
Continue until no results remain
```

This is an advanced use case and is more common with stored procedures or database-specific SQL than with ordinary CRUD queries.

sections.title: Resource Management During SQL Execution
Exception Handling During SQL Execution
Statement vs PreparedStatement
sections.content:
Statement and PreparedStatement both execute SQL, but they are intended for different use cases.

Statement:
- Suitable for simple static SQL.
- SQL is supplied directly to the statement.
- Does not provide parameter placeholders in the same way as PreparedStatement.
- Unsafe when developers construct SQL by concatenating untrusted input.

PreparedStatement:
- Designed for parameterized SQL.
- Uses ? placeholders.
- Supports typed parameter binding.
- Helps prevent SQL injection when used correctly.
- Can be useful for repeatedly executing the same SQL with different values.

Example:

```java
PreparedStatement ps = connection.prepareStatement(
    "SELECT * FROM employee WHERE id = ?"
);
ps.setLong(1, employeeId);
```

For most application CRUD operations involving values supplied at runtime, PreparedStatement is the usual choice.

sections.title: Performance Considerations
sections.content:
SQL execution performance depends on much more than the JDBC method itself. Important factors include database indexes, query design, network latency, connection pooling, transaction boundaries, result-set size, database locks, and driver behavior.

For example, fetching thousands of rows when the application needs only one row wastes resources.

Instead of:

```sql
SELECT * FROM employee;
```

prefer a query that selects the required columns and rows:

```sql
SELECT id, name
FROM employee
WHERE department = ?
LIMIT 100;
```

The exact syntax and optimization strategy depend on the database.

PreparedStatement, appropriate indexes, reasonable fetch sizes, connection pooling, and efficient SQL can all contribute to better application performance.

sections.title: Common SQL Execution Mistakes
sections.content:
Common mistakes when executing SQL through JDBC include:

1. Using Statement with concatenated user input.
2. Using executeQuery() for an operation that should return an update count.
3. Forgetting to process or close ResultSet.
4. Forgetting to close PreparedStatement or Connection.
5. Using parameter indexes starting from 0 instead of 1.
6. Selecting unnecessary columns and rows.
7. Ignoring the returned update count when it matters to application logic.
8. Holding database connections while performing unrelated slow work.
9. Executing many individual writes when batch processing would be appropriate.
10. Keeping transactions open longer than necessary.
11. Ignoring SQLException details during troubleshooting.
12. Building very large SQL strings instead of using parameters or suitable batch operations.

topics.title: Processing Results (ResultSet)
topics.description: Learn how to process database query results using JDBC ResultSet, including cursor navigation, reading columns, handling NULL values, ResultSet types and concurrency, metadata, large results, resource management, and practical patterns for mapping database rows to Java objects.

sections.title: What Is ResultSet?
How ResultSet Fits into JDBC
sections.content:
ResultSet is part of the result-processing stage of JDBC.

```text
Java Application
       |
       v
   Connection
       |
       v
PreparedStatement
       |
       v
   executeQuery()
       |
       v
   JDBC Driver
       |
       v
    Database
       |
       v
    ResultSet
       |
       v
Java Objects / Application Logic
```

The database executes the SQL, the JDBC driver receives the returned data, and ResultSet provides a standard API through which Java code can read that data.

sections.title: ResultSet Cursor
sections.content:
A ResultSet maintains a cursor that points to the current row. When a ResultSet is created, the cursor is positioned before the first row.

Calling next() moves the cursor forward by one row.

```text
Before first row
       |
       | next()
       v
    Row 1
       |
       | next()
       v
    Row 2
       |
       | next()
       v
    Row 3
       |
       | next()
       v
After last row
```

Example:

```java
while (rs.next()) {
    String name = rs.getString("name");
    System.out.println(name);
}
```

next() returns true when the cursor successfully moves to a valid row and false when there are no more rows.

sections.title: Reading Columns by Name
Reading Columns by Index
sections.content:
ResultSet also allows columns to be accessed by numeric index. JDBC column indexes start at 1, not 0.

For example:

```sql
SELECT id, name, salary FROM employee
```

The indexes are:

```text
1 -> id
2 -> name
3 -> salary
```

Java code:

```java
while (rs.next()) {
    long id = rs.getLong(1);
    String name = rs.getString(2);
    BigDecimal salary = rs.getBigDecimal(3);
}
```

Column indexes can be convenient in tightly controlled code, but column labels are often easier to maintain when queries change.

sections.title: Common ResultSet Getter Methods
sections.content:
ResultSet provides getter methods for retrieving database values as Java types.

Common methods include:

```text
getString()
getInt()
getLong()
getBoolean()
getDouble()
getBigDecimal()
getDate()
getTime()
getTimestamp()
getBytes()
getObject()
```

Example:

```java
String name = rs.getString("name");
int age = rs.getInt("age");
long id = rs.getLong("id");
BigDecimal salary = rs.getBigDecimal("salary");
Timestamp createdAt = rs.getTimestamp("created_at");
```

The selected getter should match the Java representation expected by the application and the database column type.

sections.title: Mapping a ResultSet Row to a Java Object
Handling SQL NULL Values
sections.content:
SQL NULL needs special attention because primitive Java types cannot represent null.

For example:

```java
int age = rs.getInt("age");
boolean isNull = rs.wasNull();
```

If age is SQL NULL, getInt() returns the primitive default value 0, and wasNull() can be used to determine whether the database value was actually NULL.

For nullable values, wrapper types or getObject() can make the distinction easier to represent:

```java
Integer age = rs.getObject("age", Integer.class);
```

The important point is that Java's primitive default value should not automatically be interpreted as the database value when SQL NULL is possible.

sections.title: getObject() in ResultSet
sections.content:
getObject() can retrieve a column as an Object and is useful when the application needs more flexible type handling.

```java
Object value = rs.getObject("status");
```

Modern JDBC also supports a typed form:

```java
Integer age = rs.getObject("age", Integer.class);
```

The exact Java type returned by an untyped getObject() can depend on the JDBC driver and database type. Typed getObject() can make the application's expected representation more explicit when supported by the driver.

sections.title: Checking Whether a ResultSet Contains Rows
Processing Multiple Rows
Scrollable ResultSet
sections.content:
The default ResultSet is commonly forward-only. JDBC also supports scrollable ResultSets that allow the cursor to move backward and forward when the driver and database support the requested mode.

Example:

```java
Statement statement = connection.createStatement(
    ResultSet.TYPE_SCROLL_INSENSITIVE,
    ResultSet.CONCUR_READ_ONLY
);

ResultSet rs = statement.executeQuery(
    "SELECT id, name FROM employee"
);

rs.next();
rs.next();
rs.previous();
```

Useful cursor methods include:

```text
next()
previous()
first()
last()
beforeFirst()
afterLast()
absolute()
relative()
```

Scrollable ResultSets can require additional database or driver resources, so forward-only processing is often preferable for normal application queries.

sections.title: ResultSet Types
sections.content:
JDBC defines different ResultSet cursor behaviors. The main types are:

```text
TYPE_FORWARD_ONLY
TYPE_SCROLL_INSENSITIVE
TYPE_SCROLL_SENSITIVE
```

TYPE_FORWARD_ONLY allows the cursor to move forward.

TYPE_SCROLL_INSENSITIVE allows scrolling, but changes made to the underlying data are generally not reflected in the ResultSet.

TYPE_SCROLL_SENSITIVE allows scrolling and is intended to reflect certain changes in the underlying data, subject to driver and database support.

Example:

```java
Statement statement = connection.createStatement(
    ResultSet.TYPE_SCROLL_INSENSITIVE,
    ResultSet.CONCUR_READ_ONLY
);
```

sections.title: ResultSet Concurrency
sections.content:
ResultSet also has a concurrency mode that describes whether the ResultSet is intended to be read-only or updatable.

The main modes are:

```text
CONCUR_READ_ONLY
CONCUR_UPDATABLE
```

Most application queries use read-only ResultSets:

```java
Statement statement = connection.createStatement(
    ResultSet.TYPE_FORWARD_ONLY,
    ResultSet.CONCUR_READ_ONLY
);
```

An updatable ResultSet can allow certain rows to be modified through ResultSet methods, but support and restrictions depend on the JDBC driver and database. Explicit UPDATE statements through PreparedStatement are generally more common in application code.

sections.title: Updating Data Through ResultSet
ResultSet Metadata
ResultSet and Column Aliases
sections.content:
SQL aliases can make ResultSet processing clearer, especially when joining multiple tables or calculating expressions.

SQL:

```sql
SELECT
    e.id AS employee_id,
    e.name AS employee_name,
    d.name AS department_name
FROM employee e
JOIN department d ON d.id = e.department_id
```

Java:

```java
long employeeId = rs.getLong("employee_id");
String employeeName = rs.getString("employee_name");
String department = rs.getString("department_name");
```

Using meaningful column labels can make mapping code easier to understand and reduce ambiguity when multiple tables contain columns with the same name.

sections.title: Processing Large Result Sets
Fetch Size
ResultSet and try-with-resources
ResultSet and Statement Lifecycle
sections.content:
A ResultSet is associated with the Statement or PreparedStatement that produced it. Closing the statement generally closes its current ResultSet.

A simple lifecycle is:

```text
Connection
    |
    v
PreparedStatement
    |
    v
executeQuery()
    |
    v
ResultSet
    |
    v
Read rows
    |
    v
Close ResultSet
    |
    v
Close Statement
    |
    v
Close Connection
```

try-with-resources makes the cleanup order explicit and reliable.

sections.title: ResultSet After Closing the Connection
ResultSet and Date-Time Values
Reading Binary and Large Data
Mapping Joined Query Results
ResultSet and SQL NULL with Objects
Common ResultSet Mistakes
sections.content:
Common mistakes when processing ResultSet include:

1. Forgetting to call next() before reading the first row.
2. Assuming column indexes start at 0.
3. Reading a nullable database column into a primitive without checking SQL NULL behavior.
4. Using the wrong getter for the expected database value.
5. Keeping ResultSet objects open longer than necessary.
6. Loading millions of rows into an in-memory List unnecessarily.
7. Assuming fetchSize has identical behavior across all JDBC drivers.
8. Using scrollable ResultSets when simple forward-only processing would be sufficient.
9. Assuming every database supports updatable ResultSets in the same way.
10. Forgetting to use column aliases when joined queries contain duplicate column names.
11. Returning ResultSet objects from a DAO after the associated Connection has already been closed.

sections.title: Practical ResultSet Mapping Example
ResultSet Performance Considerations
sections.content:
ResultSet processing performance depends on the query, database, network, driver, fetch behavior, and amount of data being processed.

Useful practices include:

- Select only the columns the application needs.
- Filter rows in SQL instead of loading unnecessary records.
- Use appropriate database indexes.
- Process large result sets incrementally when possible.
- Consider fetch size for large queries and measure its effect.
- Close ResultSet and other resources promptly.
- Avoid keeping a database connection open while performing unrelated application work.
- Use pagination when the application only needs a limited portion of a large dataset.

ResultSet itself is not normally the primary cause of a slow query. Database execution plans and data access patterns usually have a much larger impact.

topics.title: JDBC Metadata
topics.description: Learn how JDBC metadata APIs provide information about the database, JDBC driver, tables, columns, supported features, and query results using DatabaseMetaData and ResultSetMetaData.

sections.title: What Is Metadata in JDBC?
sections.content:
Metadata means data that describes other data or the database environment. JDBC provides metadata APIs that allow a Java application to inspect information about the database, JDBC driver, tables, columns, and query results.

JDBC mainly provides two important metadata interfaces:

```text
DatabaseMetaData
        |
        +--> Database and driver information

ResultSetMetaData
        |
        +--> Information about query-result columns
```

Metadata is useful for database tools, reporting systems, migration utilities, debugging, dynamic applications, and compatibility checks.

sections.title: Types of JDBC Metadata
sections.content:
The two metadata interfaces most commonly used in JDBC are DatabaseMetaData and ResultSetMetaData.

DatabaseMetaData describes the database and JDBC driver.

```java
DatabaseMetaData metadata = connection.getMetaData();
```

ResultSetMetaData describes the columns returned by a particular query.

```java
ResultSetMetaData metadata = resultSet.getMetaData();
```

A simple distinction is:

```text
DatabaseMetaData
    -> What database am I connected to?

ResultSetMetaData
    -> What columns did my query return?
```

ResultSetMetaData
sections.content:
ResultSetMetaData describes the columns contained in a ResultSet. It is obtained directly from the ResultSet.

```java
ResultSetMetaData metadata = rs.getMetaData();
```

It can provide information such as:

- Number of columns
- Column names
- Column labels
- SQL type
- SQL type name
- Java class name used for the column
- Precision
- Scale
- Nullability

This is particularly useful when the application needs to process query results dynamically.

sections.title: Getting the Number of Columns
Column Name vs Column Label
sections.content:
ResultSetMetaData provides both getColumnName() and getColumnLabel(). The distinction becomes important when SQL aliases are used.

For example:

```sql
SELECT name AS employee_name
FROM employee
```

The column label is generally the label exposed by the query, so:

```java
String label = metadata.getColumnLabel(1);
String name = metadata.getColumnName(1);
```

The exact behavior of column names and labels can depend on the SQL query and JDBC driver. When processing query output for display or mapping, getColumnLabel() is often the more useful method because it reflects the result column label.

sections.title: Getting Column Type
Getting Java Class Information
sections.content:
ResultSetMetaData provides getColumnClassName() to identify the Java class that the JDBC driver recommends for retrieving a particular column.

Example:

```java
String className = metadata.getColumnClassName(1);
System.out.println(className);
```

For example, a numeric database column may be mapped to a Java numeric type. The exact class mapping depends on the JDBC driver and database.

This method can be useful in generic data-processing or reporting tools.

sections.title: Precision and Scale
sections.content:
ResultSetMetaData can provide precision and scale information for numeric columns.

```java
int precision = metadata.getPrecision(1);
int scale = metadata.getScale(1);
```

For a decimal database value such as DECIMAL(12,2), precision and scale describe the total number of significant decimal digits and the number of digits after the decimal point.

The exact metadata returned can vary depending on the database and JDBC driver, so applications should avoid assuming that every database reports metadata identically.

sections.title: Checking Column Nullability
sections.content:
ResultSetMetaData provides isNullable() to describe whether a result column may contain SQL NULL values.

Example:

```java
int nullable = metadata.isNullable(1);

if (nullable == ResultSetMetaData.columnNullable) {
    System.out.println("Column may contain NULL");
}
```

JDBC defines constants such as:

```text
columnNoNulls
columnNullable
columnNullableUnknown
```

This information can be useful for generic tools and dynamic result processing.

sections.title: Building a Dynamic ResultSet Processor
DatabaseMetaData vs ResultSetMetaData
sections.content:
The two interfaces answer different questions.

```text
DatabaseMetaData
      |
      +--> Database information
      +--> Driver information
      +--> Tables
      +--> Columns
      +--> Keys
      +--> Supported features
      +--> Transaction capabilities

ResultSetMetaData
      |
      +--> Query result columns
      +--> Column labels
      +--> SQL types
      +--> Java class mappings
      +--> Precision / scale
      +--> Nullability
```

DatabaseMetaData describes the database environment, while ResultSetMetaData describes the result returned by a particular query.

sections.title: Catalogs and Schemas
sections.content:
DatabaseMetaData can expose information about catalogs and schemas, although their meaning and usage differ between database systems.

Examples of useful methods include:

```java
ResultSet schemas = metadata.getSchemas();
ResultSet catalogs = metadata.getCatalogs();
```

Applications that work across multiple database vendors should not assume that catalog and schema semantics are identical everywhere.

Metadata APIs provide a standard interface, but the database and JDBC driver determine what information is actually available and how it is represented.

sections.title: Metadata for Database Tools
sections.content:
Metadata APIs are particularly useful when building tools that need to inspect unknown databases.

For example, a database browser can use DatabaseMetaData to discover tables and columns:

```text
Connect to Database
       |
       v
DatabaseMetaData
       |
       +--> Discover schemas
       |
       +--> Discover tables
       |
       +--> Discover columns
       |
       +--> Discover primary keys
       |
       +--> Discover foreign keys
       v
Display Database Structure
```

This allows a tool to inspect a database without having its complete schema hard-coded in advance.

sections.title: Metadata and Database Portability
Metadata ResultSets
Resource Management with Metadata
Common JDBC Metadata Mistakes
sections.content:
Common mistakes include:

1. Confusing DatabaseMetaData with ResultSetMetaData.
2. Assuming JDBC column indexes start at 0 instead of 1.
3. Assuming getColumnName() always returns the same value as getColumnLabel().
4. Assuming every database reports metadata in exactly the same way.
5. Forgetting to close ResultSets returned by DatabaseMetaData methods.
6. Assuming metadata guarantees SQL portability.
7. Using dynamic metadata processing for normal business logic when strongly typed mappings would be clearer.
8. Assuming all optional database capabilities are supported just because JDBC defines a corresponding method.
9. Ignoring driver-specific behavior when building cross-database tools.

topics.title: JDBC PreparedStatement
topics.description: Learn how JDBC PreparedStatement works, how to bind parameters safely, why it is preferred over Statement, and how to use it for secure and efficient database operations.

sections.title: What is PreparedStatement?
Why Use PreparedStatement?
sections.content:
PreparedStatement solves several common problems with Statement.

The main advantages are:

- Protects against SQL injection when parameters are bound correctly.
- Makes SQL easier to read when values come from variables.
- Allows the database/driver to prepare a parameterized statement.
- Avoids repeatedly building SQL strings.
- Handles many Java-to-SQL type conversions through setter methods.
- Works naturally with batch operations and transactions.

Instead of building SQL like this:

```java
String sql = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '" + email + "'";
```

use:

```java
String sql = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = ?";
PreparedStatement ps = connection.prepareStatement(sql);
ps.setString(1, email);
```

The second approach keeps SQL structure separate from user-supplied data.

Common PreparedStatement Mistakes
sections.content:
Several mistakes appear frequently in JDBC code.

1. Using parameter index 0 instead of 1.
2. Supplying fewer values than the SQL has placeholders.
3. Supplying values in the wrong order.
4. Concatenating external input into SQL instead of binding it.
5. Trying to bind table or column names with `?`.
6. Forgetting to close PreparedStatement and ResultSet.
7. Reusing a PreparedStatement without resetting parameters correctly.
8. Assuming PreparedStatement always guarantees a performance improvement.
9. Ignoring transaction boundaries for multiple related updates.
10. Logging sensitive parameter values such as passwords or tokens.

Good JDBC code keeps SQL structure clear, binds values explicitly, closes resources reliably, and handles transactions deliberately.

topics.title: JDBC CallableStatement
topics.description: Learn how JDBC CallableStatement is used to call stored procedures and functions, handle IN, OUT, and INOUT parameters, process returned results, and manage database-specific procedure calls.

sections.title: What is CallableStatement?
Why Use CallableStatement?
sections.content:
CallableStatement is useful when application logic needs to invoke database-side procedures or functions.

Common reasons include:

- Calling existing stored procedures.
- Calling stored functions.
- Passing multiple input parameters.
- Receiving output parameters.
- Executing database-side business or data-processing logic.
- Working with legacy systems where stored procedures are already part of the architecture.
- Returning multiple results from a database operation.

It is particularly useful when the database exposes a defined procedure interface that multiple applications or services need to call.

sections.title: CallableStatement Hierarchy
sections.content:
CallableStatement is part of the standard JDBC statement hierarchy.

```text
Statement
   |
PreparedStatement
   |
CallableStatement
```

CallableStatement extends PreparedStatement, so it inherits many capabilities for parameter binding and statement execution.

The main additional capability is support for stored procedure and function calls, including registration and retrieval of OUT parameters.

sections.title: Creating a CallableStatement
JDBC Procedure Call Syntax
IN Parameters
OUT Parameters
sections.content:
An OUT parameter is produced by the stored procedure and returned to Java.

Java must register the expected SQL type before executing the procedure.

```java
CallableStatement cs = connection.prepareCall(
    "{call get_user_name(?, ?)}"
);

cs.setLong(1, 101L);
cs.registerOutParameter(2, Types.VARCHAR);

cs.execute();

String userName = cs.getString(2);
```

The important sequence is:

```text
Create CallableStatement
        ↓
Set IN parameters
        ↓
Register OUT parameters
        ↓
Execute procedure
        ↓
Read OUT parameters
```

Calling `getString(2)` before executing the procedure is not the normal usage pattern.

sections.title: INOUT Parameters
registerOutParameter()
sections.content:
`registerOutParameter()` tells JDBC that a parameter will be returned by the procedure and specifies its SQL type.

```java
cs.registerOutParameter(2, Types.INTEGER);
```

For a VARCHAR result:

```java
cs.registerOutParameter(2, Types.VARCHAR);
```

For a DECIMAL result:

```java
cs.registerOutParameter(2, Types.DECIMAL);
```

The SQL type should match the procedure's OUT parameter type as expected by the database and JDBC driver.

Some overloaded forms allow additional information, such as a type name, when required by particular SQL types or drivers.

sections.title: Reading OUT Parameter Values
Calling a Stored Function
CallableStatement with Multiple Parameters
execute() with CallableStatement
sections.content:
`execute()` is commonly used for CallableStatement because a stored procedure can potentially produce different kinds of results, including ResultSets, update counts, and OUT parameters.

```java
boolean hasResultSet = cs.execute();
```

The returned boolean indicates whether the first result is a ResultSet. If it is false, the first result may instead be an update count or there may be no results.

OUT parameters are read after the call has executed.

For a procedure where you know the operation produces a ResultSet and no special call behavior is required, driver-specific behavior and procedure design should still be considered when choosing an execution method.

CallableStatement vs PreparedStatement
sections.content:
PreparedStatement and CallableStatement both support parameter binding, but their primary purposes are different.

```text
PreparedStatement
      ↓
Parameterized SQL
      ↓
SELECT / INSERT / UPDATE / DELETE

CallableStatement
      ↓
Stored procedure/function call
      ↓
IN / OUT / INOUT / return value
```

PreparedStatement example:

```java
PreparedStatement ps = connection.prepareStatement(
    "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?"
);
ps.setLong(1, 101L);
```

CallableStatement example:

```java
CallableStatement cs = connection.prepareCall(
    "{call get_user(?)}"
);
cs.setLong(1, 101L);
```

CallableStatement is the appropriate JDBC abstraction when the database exposes a stored procedure or function that the application needs to invoke.

sections.title: CallableStatement vs Statement
Database-Specific Behavior
sections.content:
CallableStatement is standardized by JDBC, but stored procedure syntax and supported SQL features vary between database systems.

For example, MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle, SQL Server, and other databases have different procedure and function capabilities.

Differences can include:

- Procedure-call syntax.
- Function invocation syntax.
- OUT parameter support.
- REF CURSOR handling.
- Named parameter support.
- SQL type mappings.
- Multiple result behavior.
- Transaction behavior inside procedures.

The Java code should therefore follow both the JDBC specification and the documentation for the specific database and JDBC driver being used.

sections.title: CallableStatement and Database Functions
CallableStatement Parameter Metadata
Handling SQLException
Practical Stored Procedure Example
sections.content:
Consider a procedure that creates an order and returns its generated ID and status.

Conceptually:

```text
Java application
      |
      | order data
      v
CallableStatement
      |
      | CALL create_order(...)
      v
Database procedure
      |
      +---- Insert order
      |
      +---- Apply database rules
      |
      +---- Generate order ID
      |
      +---- Return status
      v
Java application
```

Java might look like:

```java
String sql = "{call create_order(?, ?, ?, ?)}";

try (CallableStatement cs = connection.prepareCall(sql)) {
    cs.setLong(1, customerId);
    cs.setBigDecimal(2, totalAmount);

    cs.registerOutParameter(3, Types.BIGINT);
    cs.registerOutParameter(4, Types.VARCHAR);

    cs.execute();

    long orderId = cs.getLong(3);
    String status = cs.getString(4);
}
```

The actual procedure definition depends on the database, but the JDBC interaction follows the same general pattern.

sections.title: Common CallableStatement Mistakes
sections.content:
Common mistakes include:

1. Using `prepareStatement()` instead of `prepareCall()` for a stored procedure.
2. Forgetting to register OUT parameters.
3. Registering an OUT parameter with the wrong SQL type.
4. Reading an OUT parameter before executing the procedure.
5. Mixing up parameter indexes.
6. Forgetting that JDBC parameter indexes start at 1.
7. Treating a stored function's return value like a normal IN parameter.
8. Assuming procedure syntax is identical across database vendors.
9. Failing to close CallableStatement or returned ResultSet objects.
10. Concatenating external input into procedure-call SQL.
11. Assuming all JDBC drivers provide identical metadata or procedure behavior.
12. Ignoring transaction boundaries when a procedure is part of a larger business operation.

sections.title: When Should You Use CallableStatement?
sections.content:
Use CallableStatement when your application needs to invoke a stored procedure or stored function through JDBC.

It is a natural choice when:

- The database already exposes stored procedures as part of its API.
- A legacy application depends heavily on database procedures.
- A database function needs to be invoked from Java.
- The operation requires OUT or INOUT parameters.
- A database-side operation intentionally encapsulates multiple SQL statements.

It is not a replacement for PreparedStatement in general application code. If you simply need to execute parameterized SQL such as SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE, PreparedStatement is usually the more direct JDBC abstraction.
